Let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be the electric-field history in the material rest frame, read componentwise in its spatial basis ([[def-em-fields]]), and let $P$ be the polarisation response declared by the model.

**(a) [Causal response]** If the kernel of [[post-em-material-closure]](c) satisfies $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$, then for every bounded continuous history $E$ the response $P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ is well defined for every $t$, bounded and continuous, linear in $E$, and causal: histories equal on $(-\infty,t_0]$ produce responses equal on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

**(b) [Transfer function and dispersion relations]** If $K$ is smooth with compact support in $(0,\infty)$, the transfer function $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1}|z|^{-2}$ for $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ (with the whole-plane bound carrying the exponential factor $e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ when $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$), and its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]](b). If $K$ is locally absolutely continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1$ and $sK\in L^1$, then $\chi$ is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, obeys the stated growth bound, and satisfies the same pair of relations; an instantaneous real part $\chi_\infty$ may be added to the model, and the relations apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty$ for $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}=\chi_\infty+\chi$.

**(c) [Finitely-subtracted and polynomial branches]** For each specified integer $n\ge1$ for which the full hypotheses of [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]] hold for the declared response transfer function, its $n$-subtracted relations apply entrywise. These hypotheses include upper-half-plane holomorphy, continuity on the closed upper half-plane, the stated boundary $C^1$ regularity, holomorphy near the real subtraction point $\omega_0$, and the order-specific growth bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le C_{jk}(1+|z|^{n-1})$ outside a compact set. The Taylor polynomial and residual are

with removable values and the boundary $C^1$ hypothesis read entrywise as in the supplier. A growth bound for one order $n_0$ permits every order $n\ge n_0$ under the same local analytic and boundary hypotheses; it does not justify lower orders for which the required growth fails. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is included only under its own decay and boundary hypotheses: $P_0=0$, $f_0=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ with the supplier's principal-value convention. The separate constitutive-polynomial branch $\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$, with real coefficients or matrices $A_j$ and $K$ satisfying the supplier's integrable causal hypotheses, is causal on histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$. Its transfer is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared $Q$ leaves the proved relations for $\chi_K$, without assuming that $Q$ is the Taylor polynomial $P_n$.

**(d) [Monochromatic work, instantaneous work and passivity]** Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^3$ and $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$. Write $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)$ for the full transfer matrix used in the response: it is $\chi(\omega)$ without an instantaneous term and $\chi_\infty+\chi(\omega)$ when the arbitrary real instantaneous matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is present. The period-averaged work per unit volume is

For the instantaneous part set $S=(\chi_\infty+\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$ and $A=(\chi_\infty-\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$, so $S^{\mathsf T}=S$ and $A^{\mathsf T}=-A$. For any real $C^1$ history its exact instantaneous work split is

[L1] Clause (a) of the response theorem: for $d\ge1$, $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{d\times d})$ and bounded continuous $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$, the convolution $P(t)=\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely for every $t$, read componentwise, with the componentwise bound $|P_j(t)|\le\sum_{k=1}^d(\sup_s|E_k(s)|)\int_0^\infty|K_{jk}(s)|\,ds$; the response is bounded and continuous, the map $E\mapsto P$ is linear, and it is causal ([[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]], clause (a)).

[L5] Clauses (b)-(d) of the response theorem: in the compact smooth-kernel branch the transfer function $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is entire with $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_1|z|^{-2}$ for $z\ne0$, $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$, and the whole-plane bound with the factor $e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ for $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$, and satisfies the principal-value dispersion relations; in the locally-absolutely-continuous integrable branch $\chi$ is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, satisfies the stated growth bound and the same relations, and an instantaneous real matrix $\chi_\infty$ is subtracted before applying them, $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}=\chi_\infty+\chi$; in the monochromatic clause, with $T=2\pi/\omega$, $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$, $P(t)=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi(\omega)e e^{-i\omega t})$, $\frac1T\int_0^TE(t)\cdot P'(t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi(\omega)e)$, and this period-averaged work is nonnegative for every $e$ if and only if $M(\omega)=(\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*)/(2i)$ satisfies $e^*M(\omega)e\ge0$ for every $e$ ([[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]], clauses (b)-(d)).

[L2] The finitely-subtracted supplier: under upper-half-plane holomorphy, continuity on the closure, boundary $C^1$ regularity away from the real subtraction point, holomorphy near it and the order-specific growth $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ outside a compact set, the Taylor polynomial $P$ and residual $f=(\chi-P)/(z-\omega_0)^n$ with removable value satisfy the two $n$-subtracted principal-value relations; the unsubtracted $n=0$ case holds with $P=0$, $f=\chi$ and growth $O(1/|z|)$; and for real coefficients $A_0,\dots,A_m$ or matrices and $K$ satisfying the integrable causal hypotheses, the response $\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$ is causal with transfer $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$, $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$, the polynomial subtraction leaving the proved relations for $\chi_K$ ([[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]]).

[L3] $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$ is the framework's positive constant; multiplying a response by the positive scalar $\varepsilon_0$ preserves the existence, boundedness, continuity, linearity and causality conclusions and rescales the monochromatic work exactly as displayed ([[def-em-si-conventions]], clause (a)).

[L4] The one-variable sum, scalar-multiple and product rules hold for differentiable maps ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]), and the Euclidean dot product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] is the symmetric positive-definite bilinear form used for the quadratic form $E\mapsto E\cdot SE$.

1.1 Since $\varepsilon_0>0$ by [L3] and $\varepsilon_0K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$ whenever $K$ is, clause (a) of the Statement is clause (a) of [L1] with $d=3$ and kernel $\varepsilon_0K$: for every bounded continuous $E$ the convolution $\int_0^\infty\varepsilon_0K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ converges absolutely for every $t$, obeys the componentwise bound with $\sup|E_k|$ and $\int|\varepsilon_0K_{jk}|$, is bounded, continuous and linear in $E$, and is causal. [A1, L1, L3]

1.2 Clause (b) is the compact smooth-kernel and integrable branches of [L5] applied to the same kernel: entireness, the reality identity $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$, the decay and whole-plane bounds and the dispersion relations in the compact branch; holomorphy on the open upper half-plane, boundary $C^1$ regularity, the growth bound and the same relations in the integrable branch. Adding the real instantaneous matrix changes the total transfer to $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}=\chi_\infty+\chi$ and leaves $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}-\chi_\infty=\chi$, to which the relations apply; no work or storage property is asserted by this analytic subtraction. [A1, L5]

1.3 Clause (c) instantiates [L2] at each declared order $n$ whose hypotheses hold; the removable values and entrywise boundary hypotheses are those of the supplier, so the $n$-subtracted pair of relations holds entrywise for $n\ge1$, and the $n=0$ case requires its own $O(1/|z|)$ decay. If the growth bound holds at $n_0$, then for $n\ge n_0$ and $|z|\ge1$ one has $1+|z|^{n_0-1}\le2(1+|z|^{n-1})$, while on $|z|\le1$ both sides are bounded by a constant, so the same local analytic and boundary hypotheses give the bound at every larger order; no lower order is thereby justified. The constitutive-polynomial branch is the last clause of [L2]: the derivative of $e^{-i\omega t}$ contributes the multiplier $(-i\omega)^j$, so the declared transfer polynomial is exactly $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$, the response is causal, and subtracting $Q$ leaves the proved relations for $\chi_K$, with no identification of $Q$ with the Taylor polynomial $P_n$. [L2]

1.5 For the instantaneous part write $\chi_\infty=S+A$ with $S$ symmetric and $A$ antisymmetric, as in the Statement. For any real $C^1$ history, the product rule of [L4] gives $\frac{d}{dt}(E\cdot SE)=2\,E\cdot S\partial_tE$, while $E\cdot AE=0$ because $(E\cdot AE)^{\mathsf T}=E\cdot A^{\mathsf T}E=-E\cdot AE$; hence $E\cdot\partial_t(\varepsilon_0\chi_\infty E)=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E\cdot SE)+\varepsilon_0E\cdot A\partial_tE$, the exact split displayed. For a periodic history the storage derivative has zero period average, and with $E=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$ the remaining average is $\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(e^*Ae)$; since $\chi_\infty$ is real, $\chi_\infty^*=\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T}$ and $(\chi_\infty-\chi_\infty^*)/(2i)=A/i$, so $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=M_K+A/i$. In the explicit example $\chi_\infty=A$ has $\chi_\infty e=(i,-1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ and $e^*\chi_\infty e=2i$ for $e=(1,i,0)^{\mathsf T}$; directly $E=(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t,0)$ and $\chi_\infty\partial_tE=\omega E$, so the work is $\varepsilon_0\omega$ at every time, while $e=(1,-i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ gives $E=(\cos\omega t,-\sin\omega t,0)$, $\chi_\infty\partial_tE=-\omega E$ and averaged work $-\varepsilon_0\omega$. More generally a real antisymmetric $A$ with $A_{jk}=a\ne0$ gives $e^*Ae=2ia\ne0$ for $e=e_j+ie_k$, so an antisymmetric instantaneous part that is nonzero fails all-amplitude passivity, and pure storage for every history requires $A=0$. [L5, L4]

Then the electrostatic boundary value problems on $\Omega_v$ are solvable in the following exact senses, and the solutions are the fields of the pure electrostatic regime [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with volume source $\rho$:
(a) [Dirichlet branch] for every $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$ there is exactly one $\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ with

and it is the unique weak $H^1$ solution with trace $g$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] for the class); the field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ ([[def-em-fields]]) is $C^\infty$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ and $(E,0)$ realises the pure electrostatic regime with source $\rho$ on the vacuum region.
(b) [Neumann branch] for every $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$ with

there is $\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline{\Omega_v})$ with $-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $\partial_\nu\varphi=g$ (outward normal $\nu$, [[def-classical-normal-derivative]]), unique up to one additive constant per connected component; the normalisation $\int_{\Omega_v^{(j)}}\varphi\,dx=0$ for every $j$ selects exactly one. The compatibility is also necessary in the sense of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](b).

(c) [Conductor reading and surface-charge realization] for the separated compact-body conductor geometry and zero-interior-volume convention of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], additionally assuming $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ ambient domain, with outer boundary data $g_0\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega)$ on $\partial\Omega$ and constants $V_j$ on the conductor surfaces $\partial D_j$ (constant functions are smooth on the compact disjoint boundary pieces), the combined datum is a special case of (a); the field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\Omega_v$ extended by $E:=0$ on the conductor satisfies the adopted distributional vacuum Maxwell equations [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]] with the source pair $(\rho_v+\sigma\,\delta_{\partial D},\,0)$, where $\sigma:=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+\in C^\infty(\partial D)$ is the constructed continuous surface-charge density, agreeing afterwards with [[pthm-em-conductor-surface-charge]] ([[def-em-weak-sources]](c), [[def-em-surface-distribution]], [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]]); the total charges $Q_j=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}n\cdot E_+\,dS$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]) are thereby determined by the data, and $\varphi$ is constant on each $\partial D_j$ with value $V_j$.

(d) [Stationary sheet charge in the vacuum region] for finitely many disjoint closed smooth interfaces $\Gamma$ strictly inside $\Omega_v$, a smooth sheet density $\sigma_\Gamma$ on them, and outer Dirichlet data $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$, there is a weak solution $\varphi\in H^1(\Omega_v)$ which is $C^\infty$ on the closure of each side of every $\Gamma$, unique by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]](c)(iii), solving the weak equation with right-hand side $\int_{\Omega_v}\rho v+\sum_\Gamma\int_\Gamma\sigma_\Gamma\,Tv$; its flux jump is $n\cdot[\varepsilon_0\nabla\varphi]=-\sigma_\Gamma$, equivalently $n\cdot[E]=\sigma_\Gamma/\varepsilon_0$ in the sign convention of [[pthm-em-fixed-vacuum-jumps]]. This is the vacuum ($\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0$) transmission branch; no dielectric coefficient is introduced.

(e) [Scope] all existence statements are the ones proved in [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]] for its stated smooth bounded domains, smooth uniformly positive coefficients (here $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0 I$), smooth data and finitely many disjoint smooth interfaces; the coefficient is the smooth positive constant $\varepsilon_0I$ on every side in the transmission clause. Excluded: nonsmooth boundaries, corners, edges, coefficient loss of regularity, prescribed total charges for conductor bodies (the free equipotential problem), unbounded exterior regions without a stated decay class, dielectric material response (belonging to the material-response page) and any measurement, apparatus or empirical claim. The theorem asserts existence of the potential, not of a physical equilibrium; the ideal conductor is the adopted model of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]].
**Given:** A bounded $C^\infty$ domain $\Omega_v$ with finitely many components, smooth $\rho$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, and the quoted data of clauses (a)-(d).

[F1] The combined elliptic boundary existence theorem: for a bounded $C^\infty$ domain $\Omega$, smooth uniformly positive coefficient $\varepsilon$ and smooth $\rho$, (a) every smooth Dirichlet datum $g$ admits exactly one weak $H^1$ solution with trace $g$, continuous in the data, $C^\infty$ on $\overline\Omega$ and pointwise satisfying $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon\nabla u)=\rho$ with the given trace; (b) every smooth conormal datum $g$ with $\int_{\Omega_j}\rho+\int_{\partial\Omega_j}g=0$ on every component admits a weak solution, unique up to componentwise constants, normalised by zero componentwise means, smooth on each closed component; (c) the transmission problem with finitely many disjoint closed smooth interfaces strictly inside $\Omega$, piecewise smooth uniformly positive $\varepsilon$, piecewise smooth $\rho$ and smooth sheet charge $\sigma$ has, with outer Dirichlet data, a unique globally $H^1$ solution that is $C^\infty$ on each closed side with equal one-sided traces, and with outer Neumann data existence exactly under the componentwise compatibility $\int_{\Omega_j}\rho+\sum_{\Gamma\subset\Omega_j}\int_\Gamma\sigma+\int_{\partial\Omega_j}g=0$, uniqueness modulo componentwise constants, smoothness on each closed side, and flux jump $n\cdot[\varepsilon\nabla u]=-\sigma$ ([[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]], [[def-classical-normal-derivative]]).

[F3] The conductor model and its vacuum geometry: in the bounded smooth ambient branch $\Omega_v$ is a bounded $C^\infty$ domain whose boundary pieces are $\partial\Omega$ and the conductor surfaces $\partial D_j$, and the model supplies the zero interior field, the connectedness requirement and the potential convention ([[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]], [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]]).

[F4] Surface-charge identities: for a model of [F3] whose field has the joint one-sided $C^1$ regularity, $n\cdot E_+=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, $n\times E_+=0$, and $Q_j=\int_{\partial D_j}\sigma\,dS=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\partial_\nu\varphi\,dS$ with $\nu=-n$ on $\partial D_j$ ([[pthm-em-conductor-surface-charge]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

[F5] Interface differentiation: for a compact embedded $C^2$ interface $S$ with unit normal $n$ from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$ and a field $F$ that is $C^1$ on each side with one-sided $C^1$ traces, the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}_{\text{piecewise}}+n\cdot[F]\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}_{\text{piecewise}}+n\times[F]\delta_S$ hold, where the bracket term is the locally integrable function equal to the classical operator on each side ([[lem-em-interface-derivatives]], [[def-em-surface-distribution]]).

[F6] The adopted distributional Maxwell equations and the jump theorem's identities: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the weak equations of [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]] are exactly the solution predicate of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e), and the stationary-sheet jump theorem gives $n\cdot[E]=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, $n\times[E]=0$ under its one-sided regularity hypotheses ([[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], [[def-em-weak-sources]], [[pthm-em-fixed-vacuum-jumps]]).

[F7] Uniqueness and compatibility: the classical and weak uniqueness and compatibility statements of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]] hold for bounded smooth vacuum domains with finitely many components, including the componentwise Neumann compatibility and the transmisson uniqueness clause ([[pthm-em-electrostatic-bvp-uniqueness]]).

[F8] A bounded smooth domain, in particular the vacuum region $\Omega_v$ of [F3], has the boundary-chart presentation of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] used by the solvability theorem [F1], with the finite boundary atlas and outward normals of that definition ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], [[def-classical-normal-derivative]]).

1.1 Dirichlet branch. By [F8] the bounded smooth domain $\Omega_v$ carries the boundary-chart presentation required by the solvability theorem [F1]. With $\varepsilon:=\varepsilon_0I$, smooth and uniformly positive on $\overline{\Omega_v}$, and smooth $\rho$, [F1](a) gives exactly one $u\in H^1(\Omega_v)$ with trace $g$, $C^\infty$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$, satisfying $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon_0\nabla u)=\rho$ pointwise and $u|_{\partial\Omega_v}=g$; the weak uniqueness in the $H^1$ class with trace $g$ is part of the same clause. Dividing by $\varepsilon_0>0$ gives $-\Delta u=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and the equation and trace displayed in (a), so $\varphi:=u$ is the asserted solution and it is unique in the stated class by [F7](a) as well. The field $E:=-\nabla\varphi$ is $C^\infty$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ and satisfies $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ by [F2], which is the fixed-time reading of the pure electrostatic regime with source $\rho$; hence $(E,0)$ realises that regime on the vacuum region. This is (a). [F1, F2, F7, F8]

1.2 Neumann branch. Let $g\in C^\infty(\partial\Omega_v)$ satisfy the componentwise compatibility of (b); with $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0I$ the conormal datum of [F1](b) is $\varepsilon_0 g$ and its compatibility $\int_{\Omega^{(j)}}\rho+\int_{\partial\Omega^{(j)}}\varepsilon_0g=0$ is exactly the displayed hypothesis, so [F1](b) gives a weak solution, $C^\infty$ on each closed component, unique up to one constant per component and normalised by zero componentwise means; after division by $\varepsilon_0$ the equation is $-\Delta\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and the conormal trace is $\partial_\nu\varphi=g$ by the definition of the conormal derivative and the classical normal derivative [F1, F2]. The necessity of the compatibility is [F7](b), whose flux identity gives $\int_{\Omega^{(j)}}\rho+\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial\Omega^{(j)}}g\,dS=0$ for any classical solution. This is (b). [F1, F2, F7]

abla\varphi]=\varepsilon_0[

No dielectric coefficient is introduced because $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_0I$ on every side. This is (d). [F1, F6, F7]

2.1 Conductor reading. Assume the bounded $C^\infty$ ambient branch with outer data $g_0$ and conductor data $V_j$. The boundary of $\Omega_v$ is the disjoint union of the compact boundary pieces $\partial\Omega,\partial D_1,\dots,\partial D_m$ [F3], and the function equal to $g_0$ on $\partial\Omega$ and to the constant $V_j$ on $\partial D_j$ is smooth on each piece, hence admissible in (a) [step 1.1]; let $\varphi$ be the resulting solution and $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\Omega_v$, extended by $E:=0$ on the conductor. Then $\varphi$ is continuous on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ with the constant trace $V_j$ on each $\partial D_j$ [F3], and $E$ has the joint one-sided $C^1$ regularity across $S=\partial D$ because $E$ is $C^\infty$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ and $0$ is smooth on the conductor side [F2]. By [F4] applied to this model, $\sigma:=\varepsilon_0\,n\cdot E_+\in C^\infty(\partial D)$ — the density $\sigma$ is continuous and its pairing is the stationary-sheet source — and $Q_j=\int_{\partial D_j}\sigma\,dS=\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial D_j}\partial_\nu\varphi\,dS$, so the total charges are determined by the data. For the distributional equations: [F5] applied on the compact embedded interface $S$ with $\Omega_-$ the conductor, $\Omega_+$ the vacuum and the normal $n$ from conductor to vacuum gives $\operatorname{div}E=\{\operatorname{div}E\}_{\text{piecewise}}+(n\cdot[E])\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}_{\text{piecewise}}+(n\times[E])\delta_S$; the piecewise parts are $\rho_v/\varepsilon_0$ on the vacuum side and $0$ on the conductor side, and $[E]=E_+$ with $n\cdot E_+=\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, $n\times E_+=0$ [F4], so the identities are exactly the adopted distributional vacuum Maxwell equations with the source pair $(\rho_v+\sigma\,\delta_{\partial D},0)$ [F6]. 3.1 Scope. All existence and regularity statements above are exactly the clauses of [F1] for the smooth bounded domains of the statement, the constant coefficient $\varepsilon_0I$, smooth data and finitely many disjoint smooth interfaces; the conductor clause additionally uses only the bounded smooth ambient branch of [F3] and the constant data there. No nonsmooth boundary, corner, edge, coefficient irregularity, prescribed-total-charge problem, unbounded exterior region without a decay class, dielectric response, measurement, apparatus or empirical claim is asserted; existence of the potential is not asserted to be a physical equilibrium, which is the adopted model of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] [F3]. This is (e). [F1, F3] ∎

regularity_scope_evidence: Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the cited weak-solvability and trace suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega_v\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain with finitely many connected components (the vacuum region of the additional bounded $C^\infty$ ambient branch of [[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]] by [[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]], or any bounded smooth domain), let $\rho$ be continuous on $\overline{\Omega_v}$ (the fixed-time volume source density, C m$^{-3}$ of [[def-em-si-conventions]]), and let $\varphi_1,\varphi_2\in C^2(\overline{\Omega_v})$ be real potentials of the pure electrostatic regime [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with fields $E_i:=-\nabla\varphi_i$ of [[def-em-fields]] and
The Laplacian convention is [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. Let $\nu$ denote the outward unit normal of $\Omega_v$ ([[def-classical-normal-derivative]]). Then:

(a) [Classical Dirichlet uniqueness] if $\varphi_1=\varphi_2$ on $\partial\Omega_v$, then $\varphi_1=\varphi_2$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$, and hence $E_1=E_2$. The conclusion holds component by component; each connected component of a bounded $C^\infty$ domain is again a bounded $C^\infty$ domain, to which the connected-domain uniqueness corollary applies.

(c) [Weak variants] (i) if $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega_v)$ ([[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]) is prescribed as a trace and $\varphi_1,\varphi_2\in H^1(\Omega_v)$ are weak solutions of the Dirichlet problem with the same trace $g$, then $\varphi_1=\varphi_2$; (ii) if the conormal data are prescribed compatibly, weak $H^1$ solutions are unique modulo constants on each connected component, and for connected $\Omega_v$ this is the normalised solution of [[lem-em-weak-neumann-and-transmission-existence]]; (iii) [sheet/transmission variant] for the finite disjoint smooth interfaces and outer Dirichlet data of [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]](c), the globally $H^1$ solution is unique, and for compatible outer Neumann data it is unique modulo componentwise constants until the componentwise means are fixed.

(d) [Physics reading and conductor case] on a star-shaped vacuum domain the curl-free $C^1$ field has an interior $C^2$ potential by [[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]]. This alone does not supply closure regularity, $H^1$ membership, a trace, or prescribed boundary data; each application of (a)-(c) additionally requires its stated regularity and identical boundary/source data. In the bounded conductor model, prescribed absolute conductor potentials $V_j$ and absolute outer Dirichlet data determine the potential and field uniquely in the admitted classical or weak class. Grounding fixes the additive constant exactly. If only relative potential differences are prescribed and the outer/reference data are also allowed to shift by the same constant, the common gauge constant is free; merely omitting outer boundary data does not establish field uniqueness.

(e) [Scope] uniqueness is conditional on the stated boundary or decay data: on an unbounded exterior region without a decay condition uniqueness fails: on $\Omega_R=\{x:|x|>R\}$ the functions $0$ and $u(x)=1-R/|x|$ are two distinct bounded harmonic functions with the same zero boundary trace and different limits at infinity, so the boundary, decay and regularity hypotheses above cannot be dropped. No existence is inferred from uniqueness; the classical branch requires $C^2$ up to the closure, the weak branches carry their own domain, coefficient and trace hypotheses, and no dielectric material coefficient or empirical claim is included. For the admitted conductor class with connected vacuum, fixed absolute conductor potentials and identical outer Neumann data also give exact uniqueness: this is a mixed boundary problem with a nonempty Dirichlet part, so there is no surviving additive constant. Existence for those mixed data is not asserted here. In that weak mixed branch, write $\mathcal V_D=\{v\in H^1(\Omega_v):Tv=0\text{ on }\partial D\}$. The compared potentials have the same prescribed conductor trace and satisfy $\varepsilon_0\int_{\Omega_v}\nabla v\cdot\nabla\varphi=\int_{\Omega_v}\rho v+\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,Tv$ for every $v\in\mathcal V_D$, with the same smooth outer normal datum $g$.

**Given:** A bounded $C^\infty$ domain $\Omega_v$ with finitely many connected components, a continuous $\rho$ on $\overline{\Omega_v}$, classical potentials $\varphi_i\in C^2(\overline{\Omega_v})$ with $-\Delta\varphi_i=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ on $\Omega_v$ and fields $E_i=-\nabla\varphi_i$, all in the pure electrostatic regime with the SI constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

[F1] Classical Dirichlet and Neumann uniqueness and flux compatibility: for a bounded connected $C^1$ domain with $u_1,u_2\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$, equal $-\Delta u_i$ and equal Dirichlet traces imply $u_1=u_2$ on the closure; equal $-\Delta u_i$ and equal outward normal derivatives imply $u_1-u_2$ constant; and for a solution $-\Delta u=f$, $\partial_\nu u=g$ one necessarily has $\int_\Omega f=-\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,dS$ ([[cor-classical-dirichlet-and-poisson-problems-are-unique]], [[lem-neumann-compatibility-from-the-divergence-theorem]]).

[F2] Componentwise Neumann uniqueness: if a bounded $C^1$ domain has finitely many connected components and $u,v\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ solve the same Poisson equation with the same outward normal derivative on $\partial\Omega$, then $u-v$ is constant on each connected component ([[cor-neumann-solutions-are-unique-modulo-componentwise-constants]]).

[F3] Components of a bounded smooth domain are again bounded smooth domains: each connected component $U$ of $\Omega_v$ is an open bounded $C^k$ domain and its boundary is a union of compact pieces of $\partial\Omega_v$ ([[lem-em-vacuum-region-of-conductors-is-a-bounded-smooth-domain]](d)); adding constants preserves the Poisson equation and the normal derivative ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-classical-normal-derivative]]).

[F4] Weak Dirichlet uniqueness with prescribed trace: for a bounded $C^1$ domain and prescribed $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$ there is exactly one $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with trace $g$ solving the weak Dirichlet problem; in particular two weak solutions with the same trace and data coincide ([[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]], [[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]).

[F5] Weak Neumann existence and uniqueness: a weak Neumann solution with data $\ell$ exists exactly when $\ell(1)=0$ and is then unique up to an additive constant, the normalisation $\int_\Omega u=0$ making it unique; on finitely many components both conditions are imposed per component; the transmission problem with sheet charge has the same uniqueness structure ([[lem-em-weak-neumann-and-transmission-existence]], [[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]).

[F6] Combined elliptic boundary existence and uniqueness: outer Dirichlet data give a globally $H^1$ transmission solution that is unique; compatible outer Neumann data give existence and uniqueness modulo componentwise constants, with zero componentwise means giving uniqueness; the smooth branch is $C^\infty$ on each closed side ([[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]](a)-(c)).

[F7] On a star-shaped open set a curl-free $C^1$ field $-E$ has an interior $C^2$ potential $\varphi$ with $\nabla\varphi=-E$ and $-\Delta\varphi=\operatorname{div}E$; no boundary regularity or normalisation at infinity is supplied ([[pthm-em-electrostatic-potential]]).

u w\,dS$ for $w\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ with the outward normal $
u$; the nonnegative integral of $|

[F10] AC and AC$_\omega$ are declared mathematical assumptions of the cited weak-solvability, trace and measure suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]); $\varepsilon_0>0$ and $\Omega_v$, $\rho$, $\varphi_i$, $E_i$ are the objects of [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] and [[def-em-fields]]; the conductor model supplies the bounded smooth ambient branch and its connectedness requirement ([[post-em-electrostatic-conductor-model]]), and the mean-zero coercivity inequality is available on each connected bounded component ([[lem-em-mean-zero-coercivity-on-a-c-one-domain]], [[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]).

1.1 Classical Dirichlet uniqueness. Let $U$ be a connected component of $\Omega_v$. By [F3] $U$ is a bounded connected $C^1$ domain with $\overline U\subseteq\overline{\Omega_v}$ and the restrictions $\varphi_i|_{\overline U}\in C^2(\overline U)$ satisfy $-\Delta(\varphi_i|_U)=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ there, with equal traces on $\partial U$ when $\varphi_1=\varphi_2$ on $\partial\Omega_v$. abla(\psi-\varphi)=
abla\psi-

regularity_scope_evidence: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ in branch (a), and the Axiom of Choice together with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as declared by its weak-solvability lemmas in branch (b) ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $c>0$ and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of the framework ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]]) with field pair $(E,B)$ and Lorenz divergence $G=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$.

(a) [All-space slab; Lorenz gauge] Let $t_0<T$ and let $(\varphi,A)$ be of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ (the restriction of a $C^\infty$ pair on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$; [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Then there is a gauge function $\chi$ of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense on $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ with $\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$, $\partial_t\chi(\cdot,t_0)=0$ and $W\chi=G$ on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$; the transformed pair $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is in Lorenz gauge on $\mathbb R^3\times(t_0,T)$, has the same field pair $(E,B)$, and any two such gauge functions differ by a solution of $W\chi=0$. This is the exact content of [[lem-em-gauge-wave-reachability]] read for potential pairs of the framework; its physical content is that every smooth potential representation of a field pair on a slab admits a Lorenz-gauge representative with zero gauge Cauchy data at $t_0$, without changing the fields.

(b) [Bounded smooth domain; Coulomb gauge with admissible boundary families] Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ graph domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an arbitrary interval, possibly unbounded, and let $(\varphi,A)$ be $C^\infty$ on an actual neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega\times\overline I$. Prescribe either (i) a Dirichlet family $g_D(p,t)$ smooth in boundary charts on a neighbourhood of $\partial\Omega\times\overline I$, or (ii) an outward conormal family $\kappa(p,t)$ with the same smoothness and the compatibility $\int_{\Omega_j}\varepsilon_0\operatorname{div}A(\cdot,t)\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega_j}\kappa(\cdot,t)\,dS=0$ for every connected component $\Omega_j$ of $\Omega$ and every $t\in I$. Then there is a gauge generator $\psi$, the restriction of one $C^\infty$ function on an actual open neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega\times\overline I$, such that $\operatorname{div}(A+\nabla\psi)=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. In case (i), $\psi(p,t)=g_D(p,t)$ on $\partial\Omega\times I$, and its restriction to $\Omega\times I$ is unique with those Dirichlet values. In case (ii), $\varepsilon_0\partial_\nu\psi(p,t)=\kappa(p,t)$ there, and imposing $\int_{\Omega_j}\psi(\cdot,t)\,dx=0$ for every component and every $t$ gives a unique generator on $\Omega\times I$; without that normalization it is unique modulo smooth time-dependent spatial constants on each component. The transformed pair $T_\psi(\varphi,A)$ is in Coulomb gauge and has the same physical field pair ([[pthm-em-gauge-invariance]]). Any two Coulomb-gauge generators differ by a function spatially harmonic at every $t$; equal Dirichlet data eliminate that residual freedom, whereas equal Neumann data leave only the componentwise constants just described. Zero Dirichlet data are the corresponding special case. Auxiliary ambient continuations away from the physical region need not be unique.

(c) [Residual freedom on star-shaped domains] Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]) and let $(\varphi,A)$, $(\tilde\varphi,\tilde A)$ be two potential pairs of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ ([[def-interval]]) with the same field pair, both in Lorenz gauge. If $I$ is non-open, these $C^2$ classes and the resulting generator use the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]]; for the physical open laboratory interval they have their ordinary $C^2$ meaning. If a degenerate $I$ is used in this branch, choose the ambient $C^2$ extensions as part of the data: the same-field and Lorenz conditions refer to these extensions on an ambient time neighbourhood before restriction, and their time jets are not determined uniquely by the restricted values alone. Then there is a gauge function $\chi$ of class $C^2$ jointly with $(\tilde\varphi,\tilde A)=T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ and $W\chi=0$ on $\Omega\times I$.

(d) [Scope] Nothing is asserted about gauge functions meeting arbitrary prescribed boundary or initial restrictions: in (a) the gauge function has zero Cauchy data at $t_0$ and no spatial boundary condition or decay, and $\Omega$ is all of $\mathbb R^3$; in (b) the datum is either a smooth time-dependent Dirichlet family or a smooth outward conormal family satisfying the stated componentwise compatibility at every physical time, with zero-mean normalization for Neumann uniqueness; the older promise of a global Lorenz gauge on a bounded domain with prescribed boundary data is explicitly outside this result. The Coulomb-gauge statement concerns the spatial divergence in the chosen inertial chart, and the instantaneous appearance of the Coulomb potential is a property of the representation, not a signal: only the field pair $(E,B)$ is physical content ([[def-em-fields]]).

**Given:** A constant $c>0$; a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of the framework with field pair $(E,B)$ and Lorenz divergence $G$; in branch (a) times $t_0<T$ and the joint class hypotheses of the Statement; in branch (b) a bounded $C^\infty$ graph domain $\Omega$, an interval $I$, the potentials on a neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega\times\overline I$, and one of the two boundary families with its compatibility; in branch (c) an open star-shaped $\Omega$, an interval $I$, and two $C^2$ pairs $(\varphi,A)$, $(\tilde\varphi,\tilde A)$ with the same field pair and both in Lorenz gauge. The choice assumptions of the two branches are as stated.

[F3] Gauge invariance: for a potential pair and a gauge function of class $C^k$ jointly with $k\ge2$, the transform has the same field pair as the original pair ([[pthm-em-gauge-invariance]]).

[F4] Gauge shift of the Lorenz divergence: for a class $C^2$ pair and a class $C^2$ generator, $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G(\varphi,A)-W\chi$ on the region of definition ([[pthm-em-lorenz-gauge-wave-form]]).

The pair $(\varphi,A)$ satisfies the hypotheses of [F5] verbatim: it is of class $C^\infty$ in the extension sense on the slab and $G$ is its Lorenz divergence, with $E,B$ its field pair in the vocabulary of [F1] and [F2]. Let $(E_0',B_0')$ be constrained data agreeing with $(E_0,B_0)$ and with $\operatorname{curl}E_0,\operatorname{curl}B_0$ on the closed ball $\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$, and let $(E',B')$ be the corresponding constructed solution of steps 1.1 and 5.1, whose scalar data for the $i$-th component of $E$ are $(E_{0,i},\dot E_{0,i})$, respectively $(E'_{0,i},\dot E'_{0,i})$, with $\dot E'_0=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0'$. On the closed ball the scalar data agree: $E_{0,i}=E'_{0,i}$ and $c^2(\operatorname{curl}B_0)_i=c^2(\operatorname{curl}B_0')_i$; the sources are $h=\tilde h=0$ on the closed backward cone $K(x_*,t_*)$, which is exactly the cone object of [F10]. Clause (c) of [F1] applied to each of the six scalar problems therefore gives $E(x_*,t_*)=E'(x_*,t_*)$ and $B(x_*,t_*)=B'(x_*,t_*)$ for every $x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and $t_*\in[t_0,T]$. For the model reading, put the event $q=(x_*,t_*)$ in the inertial chart $x^0=ct$ of [F10]; for an event $p=(y,v)$ with $t_0\le v\le t_*$ the displacement $q-p$ has components $(c(t_*-v),x_*-y)$, and by the closure description of the future cone in [F10] one has $p\le q$ if and only if $c(t_*-v)\ge|x_*-y|$, that is, $(y,v)\in K(x_*,t_*)$; hence $K(x_*,t_*)$ is the model causal past $J^-(q)$ intersected with the slab, and an event outside it cannot be joined to $q$ by a piecewise $C^1$ future causal path, since such a path has displacement in the closed future cone by [F10]. This is the modelling statement of clause (c) and carries no empirical claim. [step 1.1, step 5.1, F1, F10]

6.3 Compact support. Assume $E_0,B_0$ vanish off a compact $K$ and choose $\rho>0$ with $K\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$, which exists because compact subsets of $\mathbb R^3$ are bounded [F9]. For $x\notin K$ the fields $E_0,B_0$ vanish on a neighbourhood of $x$, so $\dot E_0=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$ and $\dot B_0=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$ vanish at $x$ as well: each component of the scalar data of step 1.1 vanishes off $K$, and $h=0$ vanishes off the compact set $\{0\}$. Fix $t\in[t_0,T]$ and $x$ with $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$; then for every $y\in\overline B_{c(t-t_0)}(x)$ the reverse triangle inequality gives $|y|\ge|x|-|y-x|>|x|-c(t-t_0)>\rho$, so $y\notin K$ and all six scalar data vanish at $y$, and $(y,v)\in K(x,t)$ likewise has $v\in[t_0,t]$, $|y-x|\le c(t-v)$ and hence $|y|\ge|x|-c(t-v)\ge|x|-c(t-t_0)>\rho$, so $h(y,v)=0$; clause (d) of [F1] applied to each component with $\rho$ and the compact $\{0\}$ therefore gives $E(x,t)=B(x,t)=0$, which is clause (d). [step 1.1, step 5.1, F1, F9, algebra]

6.4 Finite-energy setup and the flux bound. Let $u$ and $S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of [F5] for the fields of step 5.1; $u$ is a nonnegative $C^\infty$ function and $S$ a $C^\infty$ vector field, and by [F4] with $J=0$ the local Poynting identity $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=0$ holds on the whole slab. For every $x$ and $v$, the coordinate identity $|E\times B|^2=|E|^2|B|^2-(E\cdot B)^2\le|E|^2|B|^2$ of [F14] gives $|S|=\mu_0^{-1}|E\times B|\le\mu_0^{-1}|E||B|=c\,pq$ with $p=\sqrt{\varepsilon_0}|E|$ and $q=|B|/\sqrt{\mu_0}$, because $c\sqrt{\varepsilon_0\mu_0}=1$ by [F11]; since $2pq\le p^2+q^2$ for real $p,q$, $|S|\le c(p^2+q^2)/2=c\,u$. [step 5.1, F4, F5, F11, F14, algebra]

7.1 Moving-ball identity. Fix $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, $r_0>0$ and $t_0\le s\le t\le T$, put $r(v):=r_0+c(t-v)$ for $v\in[s,t]$ (so $r\ge r_0>0$ and $r'=-c$), and put $F(v):=\int_{B_{r(v)}(x_0)}u(x,v)\,dx$. For each $v$, the map $T_v(y)=x_0+r(v)y$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\det DT_v=r(v)^3$, and $T_v(B_1(0))=B_{r(v)}(x_0)$; by the change-of-variables lemma [F7] applied to the nonnegative Borel function $u(\cdot,v)$, $F(v)=\int_{B_1(0)}f(y,v)\,dy$ with $f(y,v):=u(x_0+r(v)y,v)r(v)^3$, and the boundary sphere $S^2$ is Lebesgue null by [F9], so the integral may equivalently be taken over the compact set $\overline B_1(0)$. On an open neighbourhood of $\overline B_1(0)\times[s,t]$ the function $f$ and its partial derivative $\partial_vf=\nabla u(x_0+ry,v)\cdot r'y\,r^3+\partial_vu(x_0+ry,v)\,r^3+3r^2r'u(x_0+ry,v)$ are continuous, because $u$ is $C^\infty$ in the extension sense and $r$ is $C^1$; the parameter-integral lemma [F6] with the compact finite-measure set $\overline B_1(0)$ therefore gives the one-sided derivatives at the endpoints and $F'(v)=\int_{\overline B_1(0)}\partial_vf(y,v)\,dy$ for $v\in(s,t)$. Expanding and substituting back, the first and third terms are $\int_{\overline B_1}\bigl[r^3r'\nabla u(x_0+ry,v)\cdot y+3r^2r'u(x_0+ry,v)\bigr]dy=\frac{r'}{r}\int_{B_r(x_0)}\operatorname{div}\bigl((x-x_0)u(x,v)\bigr)dx$, and the second term is $r^3\int_{\overline B_1}\partial_vu(x_0+ry,v)\,dy=\int_{B_r(x_0)}\partial_vu(x,v)\,dx$; the divergence theorem [F8] applies on the ball $B_r(x_0)$, a bounded $C^1$ domain with outward normal $n=(x-x_0)/r$, giving $\int_{B_r}\operatorname{div}\bigl((x-x_0)u\bigr)=r\int_{\partial B_r}u\,dS$ and, with $\partial_vu=-\operatorname{div}S$ from the Poynting identity of step 6.4, $\int_{B_r}\partial_vu=-\int_{\partial B_r}S\cdot n\,dS$. Hence $F'(v)=-\int_{\partial B_r(x_0)}\bigl(S\cdot n-r'(v)u\bigr)dS=-\int_{\partial B_r(x_0)}\bigl(S\cdot n+c\,u\bigr)dS$ with $r=r(v)$, and the integrand is nonnegative because $S\cdot n+cu\ge-|S|+cu\ge0$ by step 6.4; the surface integral of a nonnegative continuous function is nonnegative by the definition of the surface integral [F8], so $F'\le0$ on $(s,t)$. [step 6.4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, A1, given, algebra]

8.1 Local energy estimate and the equality. By step 7.1, $F$ is continuous on $[s,t]$ and differentiable on $(s,t)$ with $F'\le0$, so the mean value theorem [F9] gives $F(t)\le F(s)$, that is, for every $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, $r_0>0$ and $t_0\le s\le t\le T$, $\int_{B_{r_0}(x_0)}u(x,t)\,dx\le\int_{B_{r_0+c(t-s)}(x_0)}u(x,s)\,dx$; this is the local inequality of clause (e) for the constructed pair, and the computation of step 7.1 used only the nonnegativity of $u$, the Poynting identity, the bound $|S|\le cu$ and the smoothness of the pair, so the same inequality holds for every smooth source-free Maxwell solution on a slab with its own energy density and flux. Taking $s=t_0$ and the supremum over $r_0>0$ with $x_0=0$ gives $\mathcal E(t)\le\mathcal E(t_0)$ for every $t\in[t_0,T]$. For the reverse inequality, apply the same computation to the pair $\widetilde E(x,v):=E(x,t-v)$, $\widetilde B(x,v):=-B(x,t-v)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times[0,t-t_0]$: by the chain rule and the four equations of step 5.1, $\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=\operatorname{div}\widetilde B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=-\partial_v\widetilde B$ and $\operatorname{curl}\widetilde B=c^{-2}\partial_v\widetilde E$, so the pair is a smooth source-free solution on that slab, with energy density $u(x,t-v)$ and Poynting vector $-S(x,t-v)$; applying the local inequality with $s'=0$ and $t'=t-t_0$ gives $\int_{B_{r_0}(x_0)}u(x,t_0)\,dx\le\int_{B_{r_0+c(t-t_0)}(x_0)}u(x,t)\,dx\le\mathcal E(t)$ for every $r_0$, so $\mathcal E(t_0)\le\mathcal E(t)$. Hence if $\mathcal E(t_0)<\infty$ then $\mathcal E(t)=\mathcal E(t_0)$ for every $t\in[t_0,T]$. [step 5.1, step 7.1, F9, algebra]

9.1 Conclusion. Steps 1.1, 5.1 prove clause (a) with the explicit spherical-mean representation, step 6.1 proves clause (b), step 6.2 proves clause (c) including the model cone reading, step 6.3 proves clause (d), and steps 6.4, 7.1 and 8.1 prove clause (e) with the local estimate and the total-energy equality under $\mathcal E(t_0)<\infty$. Clause (f) records the scope: the argument is conditional on the adopted postulates and on $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, which is used in step 1.1 through [F1], in step 7.1 through the change-of-variables and divergence suppliers [F7, F8] and the parameter-integral lemma [F6], and in step 8.1 through the same suppliers applied to the time-reversed pair; no decay, boundedness, compactness or finite-energy hypothesis was imposed on the data of the arbitrary-growth branch, no boundary condition, inhomogeneous source or weak-branch content is asserted, and the conclusion makes no empirical claim. [step 1.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 6.2, step 6.3, step 6.4, step 7.1, step 8.1, given] ∎

1.2 For the patch identities of (a), fix a patch test geometry $(D,r)$ and put $S=r[D]$, with parameter derivatives $r_u,r_v$ and oriented area vector $r_u\times r_v$. The flux functions $\Phi_B(t):=\int_D\langle B(r(u,v),t),r_u(u,v)\times r_v(u,v)\rangle\,dudv$ and $\Phi_E$ are differentiable on $I$ with $\Phi_B'(t)=\int_S\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and $\Phi_E'(t)=\int_S\partial_tE(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$: the integrands are the continuous functions $\langle B(r(u,v),t),r_u\times r_v\rangle$ with continuous $t$-derivative $\langle\partial_tB(r(u,v),t),r_u\times r_v\rangle$ on a neighbourhood of the compact Jordan region $D$ times a compact interval around $t$, [F6] identifies the Riemann integral with the Lebesgue integral, and [F7] differentiates under the integral. Stokes' theorem [F5] applied to the $C^1$ fields gives $\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_S\operatorname{curl}E(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS$ and the corresponding identity for $B$, in the induced orientation of the patch; substituting the Faraday law $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ of [F1] gives $\oint_{\partial S}E(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=-\int_S\partial_tB(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS=-\Phi_B'(t)$, and substituting the Ampere law gives $\oint_{\partial S}B(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r=\mu_0\int_SJ(\cdot,t)\cdot n_S\,dS+c^{-2}\Phi_E'(t)$. [F1, F2, F5, F6, F7, given, algebra]

1.3 For clause (b), fix a closed axis-parallel box $K=\prod_{i<3}[a_i,b_i]\subseteq\Omega$ with $a_i<b_i$ and let $V$ be its open interior, a volume test geometry with $\overline V=K$ by [F2]. The volume identity hypothesis and the divergence theorem give $0=\oint_{\partial V}E(\cdot,t)\cdot\nu_V\,dS-(1/\varepsilon_0)\int_V\rho(\cdot,t)\,d\lambda_3=\int_Vh\,d\lambda_3$ for the continuous function $h:=\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0$, where linearity [F9] combines the two finite integrals and [F4] identifies the flux with $\int_V\operatorname{div}E$; by [F2] and [F9] this equals $\int_Kh\,d\lambda_3$, because $K\setminus V$ is $\lambda_3$-null. Since every closed axis-parallel box $K\subseteq\Omega$ with positive sides arises this way, [F8] with $n=3$ gives $h=0$ on $\Omega$, that is $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$. The same computation with the second volume identity and $\int_V\operatorname{div}B=0$ gives $\operatorname{div}B=0$. [F1, F2, F4, F8, F9, given, algebra]

1.4 For the curl equations fix a point $p\in\Omega$ and let $(j,k)$ be the cyclic pair with $e_j\times e_k=e_i$ for a coordinate index $i$. Put $W:=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:p+ue_j+ve_k\in\Omega\}$, an open set, and $\varphi_i(u,v):=\bigl(\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB\bigr)(p+ue_j+ve_k)\cdot e_i$ on $W$, a continuous function. For every closed axis-parallel square $Q\subseteq W$ with side $\ell>0$ the affine patch $r(u,v):=p+ue_j+ve_k$ over $Q$ is a patch test geometry with $r_u\times r_v=e_i$ and image in $\Omega$; Stokes [F5], the differentiability of its flux function and the Faraday identity of the hypothesis give $\int_Q\varphi_i\,dudv=\int_Q\langle(\operatorname{curl}E)\circ r,r_u\times r_v\rangle\,dudv+\frac{d}{dt}\int_Q\langle B\circ r,r_u\times r_v\rangle\,dudv=\oint_{\partial S}E\cdot d\mathbf r+\frac{d}{dt}\int_SB\cdot n_S\,dS=0$. Hence the continuous function $\varphi_i$ has vanishing integral over every closed axis-parallel square contained in $W$, so the planar clause of [F8] gives $\varphi_i=0$ on $W$. The point $p\in\Omega$ was chosen arbitrarily, and $(0,0)\in W$ because $p\in\Omega$, so evaluating at $(0,0)$ gives $(\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB)(p)\cdot e_i=0$ for every $p\in\Omega$; letting $i$ run over the three coordinate indices, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ on $\Omega$. The same argument with the Ampere identity in place of Faraday gives $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$, the flux derivative producing $c^{-2}\Phi_E'$. [F2, F3, F5, F6, F7, F8, given, algebra]

regularity_scope_evidence: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as carried by the cited point-source suppliers. Let the laboratory region, chart and units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], let $q\in\mathbb R$, let $z,v_*$ be a retarded point-geometry datum of [[def-em-retarded-point-geometry]] (prescribed $C^3$ uniformly subluminal worldline, $C:=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$), let $s_0$ be an emission event with $z'(s_0)=0$ (the charge is momentarily at rest in the laboratory chart), and put $a:=z''(s_0)$ and, for $n\in S^2$, $x_r:=z(s_0)+rn$, $t_r:=s_0+r/c$. Let $E,B$ be the retarded fields of the charge given by [[pthm-em-lienard-wiechert]] and $S:=E\times B/\mu_0$ ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]]). Then:

(a) [Field on the emitted sphere] For every $r>0$ and $n\in S^2$, $$E(x_r,t_r)=\frac{C\,n\times(n\times a)}{c^2r}+\rho_E(s_0,n,r),\qquad|\rho_E(s_0,n,r)|\le|C|\frac{1+v_*/c}{(1-v_*/c)^3}r^{-2},\qquad B(x_r,t_r)=\frac{n\times E(x_r,t_r)}{c}.$$

(b) [Angular flux density] The limits $$\frac{dP}{d\sigma}(n):=\lim_{r\to\infty}r^2\,n\cdot S(x_r,t_r)=\frac{C^{2}\,|n\times(n\times a)|^{2}}{\mu_0c^{5}},\qquad P_{\mathrm{em}}(s_0):=\int_{S^2}\frac{dP}{d\sigma}(n)\,d\sigma(n),$$ exist with the convergence uniform in $n\in S^2$; $d\sigma$ is the polar surface measure of the unit sphere (equal to the chart surface measure by [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).
(c) [Total power] $$P_{\mathrm{em}}(s_0)=\frac{C^{2}}{\mu_0c^{5}}\cdot\frac{8\pi}{3}|a|^{2}=\frac{q^2|a|^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^{3}},$$ the Larmor power of the momentarily resting prescribed charge.

(d) [Angular distribution] Writing $\theta$ for the angle between $n$ and $a$ (with $\theta$ undefined only when $a=0$, in which case $dP/d\sigma\equiv0$), $$\frac{dP}{d\sigma}(n)=\frac{q^2|a|^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0c^{3}}\sin^2\theta:$$ the radiation pattern vanishes along the instantaneous acceleration axis and is maximal in the perpendicular plane; $\int_{S^2}dP/d\sigma\,d\sigma=P_{\mathrm{em}}(s_0)$. If $a=0$ all displayed radiation quantities vanish.

(f) [General low-speed branch] At any emission event, without imposing $z'(s_0)=0$ for this clause, define emitted power by the weighted far-zone flux integral $\kappa_0(n)\,r^2\,n\cdot S$ on the emitted spheres, with $\kappa_0(n)=1-n\cdot\beta_0$, $\beta_0=z'(s_0)/c$ and $|\beta_0|\le v_*/c$. The same field formula and angular computation give $$P_{\mathrm{em}}=\gamma_0^{6}\bigl(|a|^{2}-|\beta_0\times a|^{2}\bigr)\frac{q^{2}}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^{3}}.$$ Put $P_{\mathrm L}=q^{2}|a|^{2}/(6\pi\varepsilon_0c^{3})$. For $|\beta_0|\le\delta<1$, $$P_{\mathrm L}\le P_{\mathrm{em}}\le(1-\delta^{2})^{-3}P_{\mathrm L},\qquad |P_{\mathrm{em}}-P_{\mathrm L}|\le3\delta^{2}(1-\delta^{2})^{-3}P_{\mathrm L}.$$ This includes $q=0$ or $a=0$ without division by $P_{\mathrm L}$. Uniform angular comparison is also explicit: if $N_\beta=n\times((n-\beta_0)\times a)$, $N_0=n\times(n\times a)$ and $H_\beta=q^{2}|N_\beta|^{2}/(16\pi^{2}\varepsilon_0c^{3}\kappa_0^{5})$, $H_0=q^{2}|N_0|^{2}/(16\pi^{2}\varepsilon_0c^{3})$, then $$|H_\beta-H_0|\le\frac{q^2|a|^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0c^3}\,\delta\left[\frac{2+\delta}{(1-\delta)^5}+\frac{5}{(1-\delta)^6}\right]$$ for all $n$. The exact rest-event clauses (a)-(e) retain their hypotheses; this additional branch supplies the general low-speed comparison, not a mechanical loss law.
[F8] SI relations: $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, $C^2/(\mu_0c^5)=q^2/(16\pi^2\varepsilon_0c^3)$, since $\varepsilon_0\mu_0c^2=1$. ([[def-em-si-conventions]])

[F9] One-variable calculus: the second fundamental theorem for continuous derivatives, the chain and power rules and the derivative of $y^m$ for integers $m$, and the mean value theorem; together with the continuity of the power functions on their domains. ([[thm-ftc-second-part]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]])

1.1 Field on the emitted sphere (a). At the rest event $z'(s_0)=0$, so at the emitted sphere the retarded data are $\beta=0$, $\kappa=1$, $\dot\beta=a/c$ [F2]; [F1] then gives $E_{\mathrm{vel}}=C(1-0)(n-0)/(1\cdot r^{2})=Cn/r^{2}$ and $E_{\mathrm{acc}}=C\,n\times((n-0)\times a/c)/(c\cdot1\cdot r)=C\,n\times(n\times a)/(c^{2}r)$, together with $B=n\times E/c$. Writing $\rho_E:=Cn/r^{2}$ gives $E(x_r,t_r)=C\,n\times(n\times a)/(c^{2}r)+\rho_E$ and $|\rho_E|=|C|/r^{2}\le|C|(1+v_*/c)(1-v_*/c)^{-3}r^{-2}$, because both factors in the last expression are at least $1$. This is (a). [F1, F2, F8, algebra]

2.1 Angular flux limit (b). Write $E(x_r,t_r)=E_{\mathrm{lead}}+\rho_E$ with $E_{\mathrm{lead}}:=C\,n\times(n\times a)/(c^{2}r)$ and $|\rho_E|\le D_E r^{-2}$, where $D_E:=|C|(1+v_*/c)(1-v_*/c)^{-3}$ [step 1.1]. Since $B=n\times E/c$, the identity $n\cdot(E\times(n\times E))=|n\times E|^{2}$ of [F4] gives $n\cdot S=n\cdot(E\times B)/\mu_0=|n\times E|^{2}/(\mu_0c)$. Now $|n\times E_{\mathrm{lead}}|=C|n\times(n\times(n\times a))|/(c^{2}r)=C|n\times a|/(c^{2}r)$ and $|n\times a|=|n\times(n\times a)|$ by [F4], so $$r^{2}n\cdot S=\frac{C^{2}|n\times(n\times a)|^{2}}{\mu_0c^{5}}+R_r(n),\qquad |R_r(n)|\le r^{2}\frac{2|n\times E_{\mathrm{lead}}||n\times\rho_E|+|n\times\rho_E|^{2}}{\mu_0c}\le\frac{K}{r}$$ for all $r\ge1$ and all $n\in S^2$, with $K:=2C|a|D_E/(\mu_0c^{3})+D_E^{2}/(\mu_0c)$ independent of $n$ and $r$ [F6]. Hence $r^{2}n\cdot S\to C^{2}|n\times(n\times a)|^{2}/(\mu_0c^{5})$ uniformly in $n$; the limit function is continuous on $S^2$, and $\int_{S^2}|R_r|\,d\sigma\le K r^{-1}\sigma(S^2)\to0$, so by [F6] and [F7] $\int_{S^2}r^{2}n\cdot S\,d\sigma$ converges to $\frac{C^{2}}{\mu_0c^{5}}\int_{S^2}|n\times(n\times a)|^{2}d\sigma$. By [F10] the chart surface measure may be read as the polar measure $d\sigma$. This is (b), including the finiteness and continuity of $dP/d\sigma$. [step 1.1, F4, F6, F7, F10, algebra]

3.1 Total power (c). By [F4], $|n\times(n\times a)|^{2}=|n\times a|^{2}=|a|^{2}-(n\cdot a)^{2}$; integrating over $S^2$ with [F3] gives $\int_{S^2}|n\times(n\times a)|^{2}d\sigma=4\pi|a|^{2}-(4\pi/3)|a|^{2}=(8\pi/3)|a|^{2}$. Substituting into step 2.1, $P_{\mathrm{em}}=\frac{C^{2}}{\mu_0c^{5}}\cdot\frac{8\pi}{3}|a|^{2}$; and $\frac{C^{2}}{\mu_0c^{5}}=\frac{q^{2}}{16\pi^{2}\varepsilon_0^{2}\mu_0c^{5}}=\frac{q^{2}}{16\pi^{2}\varepsilon_0c^{3}}$ by [F8] (using $\varepsilon_0\mu_0c^{2}=1$), so $P_{\mathrm{em}}=\frac{q^{2}|a|^{2}}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^{3}}$. This is (c). [step 2.1, F3, F4, F8, algebra]

4.1 Angular distribution (d). Let $\theta$ be the angle between $n$ and $a$ when $a\ne0$. By [F4], $|n\times(n\times a)|^{2}=|a|^{2}-(n\cdot a)^{2}=|a|^{2}(1-\cos^{2}\theta)=|a|^{2}\sin^{2}\theta$; since $\sin^{2}\theta=0$ exactly for $\theta\in\{0,\pi\}$ [F9], the pattern vanishes precisely along $\pm a$ and is maximal where $\sin^{2}\theta=1$, i.e. in the plane perpendicular to $a$; its coefficient is $\frac{C^{2}}{\mu_0c^{5}}=\frac{q^{2}}{16\pi^{2}\varepsilon_0c^{3}}$ [F8]. If $a=0$, then $|n\times(n\times 0)|^{2}=0$ for every $n$, so $dP/d\sigma\equiv0$ and $P_{\mathrm{em}}=0$ by (c). Finally $\int_{S^2}\frac{dP}{d\sigma}d\sigma=P_{\mathrm{em}}(s_0)$ is (c). This is (d). [step 2.1, step 3.1, F3, F4, F8, F9, algebra]

5.1 General far-zone limit and weighted power (f, first part). Now let $s_0$ be an arbitrary emission event with $\beta_0:=z'(s_0)/c$, $|\beta_0|\le v_*/c$, and $a:=z''(s_0)$; the same computation as steps 1.1-2.1 applies with $\beta_0$ in place of $0$ and $\kappa_0$ in place of $1$ [F2]. By [F1], $E_{\mathrm{lead}}:=C\,n\times((n-\beta_0)\times a)/(c^{2}\kappa_0^{3}r)$ is the acceleration part and $E_{\mathrm{vel}}$ is the remainder with $|E_{\mathrm{vel}}|\le D_Er^{-2}$; writing $N_\beta:=n\times((n-\beta_0)\times a)$ and repeating the flux identity of step 2.1, $r^{2}n\cdot S=\frac{C^{2}|N_\beta|^{2}}{\mu_0c^{5}\kappa_0^{6}}+R_r(n)$ with $|R_r(n)|\le K'r^{-1}$ for $r\ge1$, uniformly in $n$ and with $K'$ independent of $n$; here $1-\delta\le\kappa_0\le1+\delta$ keeps every power of $\kappa_0$ bounded on the compact $S^2$ [F2, F6]. Hence $\kappa_0(n)\,r^{2}n\cdot S\to H_\beta(n):=\frac{C^{2}|N_\beta|^{2}}{\mu_0c^{5}\kappa_0^{5}}$ uniformly, and the weighted emitted power $P_{\mathrm{em}}:=\int_{S^2}\kappa_0\lim_{r\to\infty}(r^{2}n\cdot S)\,d\sigma=\frac{C^{2}}{\mu_0c^{5}}\int_{S^2}\frac{|N_\beta|^{2}}{\kappa_0^{5}}\,d\sigma$ is the dominated-convergence limit of the weighted fluxes, the weight $\kappa_0$ being bounded and continuous [F6, F7]. [step 2.1, step 4.1, F1, F2, F6, F7, algebra]

6.1 Evaluation of the weighted angular integral (f, second part). By [F4], $N_\beta=(n\cdot a)(n-\beta_0)-(1-n\cdot\beta_0)a$, so with $b:=|\beta_0|\in[0,v_*/c)$ and $u:=n\cdot\beta_0/b$ (any unit vector $e_3$ along $\beta_0$ when $b>0$; the case $b=0$ is step 3.1) one gets $$|N_\beta|^{2}=-(1-b^{2})(n\cdot a)^{2}+2(1-bu)b\,a_\parallel(n\cdot a)+(1-bu)^{2}|a|^{2},$$ where $a_\parallel$ is the component of $a$ along $\beta_0$. Averaging the $\varphi$-dependence over the sphere with [F3] (the linear term in the tangential component of $n$ integrates to $0$, and the square of that component integrates to $\pi\int(1-u^{2})f$), the parallel coefficient of $|N_\beta|^{2}/(1-bu)^{5}$ reduces to $1-u^{2}$ and the perpendicular coefficient to $(1-bu)^{2}-\tfrac{1-b^{2}}{2}(1-u^{2})$. Hence, with $J_5:=\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^{2})(1-bu)^{-5}du$ and $J_3:=\int_{-1}^{1}(1-bu)^{-3}du$, $$\int_{S^2}\frac{|N_\beta|^{2}}{\kappa_0^{5}}d\sigma=2\pi a_\parallel^{2}J_5+2\pi a_\perp^{2}\Bigl[J_3-\frac{1-b^{2}}{2}J_5\Bigr].$$ The substitution $y=1-bu$ (for $b>0$, with $du=-dy/b$) and the second fundamental theorem [F9], with the antiderivatives $-y^{-2}/2$ and $b^{-3}\bigl[(1-b^{2})y^{-4}/4-2y^{-3}/3+y^{-2}/2\bigr]$, give $J_3=2/(1-b^{2})^{2}$ and $J_5=4/(3(1-b^{2})^{3})$; at $b=0$ the same formulas follow by direct integration ($J_3=2$, $J_5=4/3$) and all expressions are continuous in $b$, so no division by $b$ is needed in the conclusion. Therefore $$\int_{S^2}\frac{|N_\beta|^{2}}{\kappa_0^{5}}d\sigma=\frac{8\pi}{3}\Bigl[a_\parallel^{2}(1-b^{2})^{-3}+a_\perp^{2}(1-b^{2})^{-2}\Bigr]=\frac{8\pi}{3}\gamma_0^{6}\bigl(|a|^{2}-|\beta_0\times a|^{2}\bigr),$$ because $(1-b^{2})^{-1}=\gamma_0^{2}$, $(1-b^{2})^{-3}=\gamma_0^{6}$ and $|a|^{2}-|\beta_0\times a|^{2}=a_\parallel^{2}+(1-b^{2})a_\perp^{2}$ by [F4]. Substituting into step 5.1 and converting the constant with [F8] gives $P_{\mathrm{em}}=\gamma_0^{6}(|a|^{2}-|\beta_0\times a|^{2})\frac{q^{2}}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^{3}}$, the displayed general formula. [step 5.1, F3, F4, F8, F9, algebra]

7.1 Uniform low-speed comparisons (f, third part). Write $P_{\mathrm L}=q^{2}|a|^{2}/(6\pi\varepsilon_0c^{3})$ and $P_{\mathrm{em}}=\gamma_0^{6}(a_\parallel^{2}+\gamma_0^{-2}a_\perp^{2})\frac{q^{2}}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^{3}}$ [step 6.1]. Since $\gamma_0\ge1$, one has $\gamma_0^{6}a_\parallel^{2}\ge a_\parallel^{2}$ and $\gamma_0^{4}a_\perp^{2}\ge a_\perp^{2}$, so $P_{\mathrm{em}}\ge P_{\mathrm L}$; and $\gamma_0^{6}a_\parallel^{2}+\gamma_0^{4}a_\perp^{2}\le\gamma_0^{6}|a|^{2}$, so $P_{\mathrm{em}}\le\gamma_0^{6}P_{\mathrm L}$. If $b=|\beta_0|\le\delta<1$ then $\gamma_0^{2}=(1-b^{2})^{-1}\le(1-\delta^{2})^{-1}$, hence $P_{\mathrm L}\le P_{\mathrm{em}}\le(1-\delta^{2})^{-3}P_{\mathrm L}$. Moreover $P_{\mathrm{em}}-P_{\mathrm L}=\bigl[(\gamma_0^{6}-1)a_\parallel^{2}+(\gamma_0^{4}-1)a_\perp^{2}\bigr]\frac{q^{2}}{6\pi\varepsilon_0c^{3}}\le(\gamma_0^{6}-1)P_{\mathrm L}\le\bigl[(1-\delta^{2})^{-3}-1\bigr]P_{\mathrm L}\le3\delta^{2}(1-\delta^{2})^{-3}P_{\mathrm L}$, where the last step is the elementary inequality $(1-t)^{-3}-1\le3t(1-t)^{-3}$ at $t=\delta^{2}$; all these inequalities are valid also when $a=0$ or $q=0$, with both sides zero, and no division by $P_{\mathrm L}$ is performed. For the angular comparison fix $n$ and use coordinates with $n=e_3$: writing $p=(a_1,a_2)$, $q=(\beta_{0,1},\beta_{0,2})$, $t=a_3$ and $\beta_{0,3}$, one has $N_0=-p$ and $N_\beta=-(\kappa_0p+tq)$ by [F4], so with $D:=|N_\beta|^{2}\kappa_0^{-5}-|N_0|^{2}$, $$D=|p|^{2}(\kappa_0^{-3}-1)+2\kappa_0^{-4}t(p\cdot q)+\kappa_0^{-5}t^{2}|q|^{2}.$$ Since $1-\delta\le\kappa_0\le1+\delta$, the mean value theorem [F9] gives $|\kappa_0^{-3}-1|\le3\delta(1-\delta)^{-4}$ and $|\kappa_0^{-4}|\le(1-\delta)^{-4}$, $\kappa_0^{-5}\le(1-\delta)^{-5}$; also $|q|\le\delta$ and $|p|,|t|\le|a|$, and $2|t||p|\le|t|^{2}+|p|^{2}$. Hence $|D|\le|a|^{2}\bigl[4\delta(1-\delta)^{-4}+\delta^{2}(1-\delta)^{-5}\bigr]$, and this is at most $|a|^{2}\delta\bigl[(2+\delta)(1-\delta)^{-5}+5(1-\delta)^{-6}\bigr]$ because, after dividing by $\delta(1-\delta)^{-4}$, the inequality reduces to $4-3\delta\le2+\delta+5(1-\delta)^{-1}$, whose left side is at most $4$ and whose right side exceeds $5$. Multiplying by $\frac{q^{2}}{16\pi^{2}\varepsilon_0c^{3}}$ gives the displayed bound on $|H_\beta-H_0|$. [step 6.1, F2, F4, F9, algebra]

8.1 Scope and conclusion (e). At a rest event $z'(s_0)=0$ one has $\kappa_0(n)=1-n\cdot 0=1$ for every $n\in S^2$ [F2], so the emission-time Jacobian is identically $1$ and no retarded-time conversion factor appears: the limits of (b) are simultaneously the fixed-sphere flux and the emitted power per unit emission time, and the angular and total powers of (c)-(d) are the emitted quantities of the rest event. The computation used only the prescribed worldline, the retarded model fields and the adopted causal selection of [[pthm-em-lienard-wiechert]] and [[post-em-radiation-selection]]; it forms no product of distributions, asserts no self-force, radiation reaction, mass derivation or mechanical evolution law, and makes no empirical or measurement claim, while clause (f) records the general low-speed comparison as a separate quantified statement rather than a loss law. Steps 1.1-7.1 together with this clause prove (a)-(f). [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 7.1, F2, F5, F10, algebra] ∎

Let $(\varphi,A)$ be the retarded history pairings of [[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]](b) -- the framework's retarded construction for this source under the adopted selection [[post-em-radiation-selection]] -- and define $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B:=\nabla\times A$ on the off-worldline domain $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]]). Then:

(b) [Exact fields] On $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, $$E=E_{\mathrm{vel}}+E_{\mathrm{acc}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{vel}}=\frac{C(1-|\beta|^2)(n-\beta)}{\kappa^3r^2},\qquad E_{\mathrm{acc}}=\frac{C\,n\times\bigl((n-\beta)\times\dot\beta\bigr)}{c\,\kappa^3r},\qquad B=\frac{n\times E}{c},$$ and $E,B$ are of class $C^1$ there; the velocity part obeys $|E_{\mathrm{vel}}|\le|C|(1+v_*/c)(1-v_*/c)^{-3}r^{-2}$.

(e) [Constructed weak solution] Let $\Phi,\Upsilon$ be the global regular potential distributions in (a), and let $\mathcal E=-\nabla\Phi-\partial_t\Upsilon$, $\mathcal B=\operatorname{curl}\Upsilon$. By [[thm-em-retarded-point-distributional-maxwell]], their representatives are exactly the locally integrable zero extensions of the displayed off-worldline fields. They satisfy all four identities of [[def-em-weak-sources]](e) with the proper all-time point pair $\rho,J$; the volume source parts are zero. Thus they are an admitted point-source model of the explicit physical adoption [[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]], under the same retarded selection. The potentials satisfy $W\Phi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $W\Upsilon=\mu_0J$ and the distributional Lorenz identity. This existence and solution property is supplied by the mathematical theorem, not by the selection postulate or by the compact-source theorem. The zero extensions on the null graph give no physically defined self-field and no nonlinear products there. All original exact field, regularity and uniform far-zone branches remain as stated. On each product neighborhood disjoint from $\Gamma$ the fields satisfy the smooth source-free Maxwell equations. Consequently any use of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] by the radiation items is local on such neighborhoods, with $\rho=J=0$; it neither applies that smooth theorem across the point source nor forms self-work or a global finite-energy identity.

**Given:** $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the laboratory chart, units and constants of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]; a retarded point-geometry datum: $q\in\mathbb R$, $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^3$ with $|z'(s)|\le v_*<c$, and the off-worldline domain $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ with the retarded data $s,r,n,\beta,\kappa,\dot\beta$ of [[def-em-retarded-point-geometry]]; the constant $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$.

[F1] Retarded point geometry: on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ the root $s=s(x,t)<t$ solves $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, is $C^3$, satisfies $\partial_ts=1/\kappa$ and $\nabla_xs=-n/(c\kappa)$, and $\kappa=1-n\cdot\beta\in[1-v_*/c,1+v_*/c]$; at an emission event $s_0$ and direction $n\in S^2$, the event $(x_r,t_r)=(z(s_0)+rn,s_0+r/c)$ lies in $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ and has root $s(x_r,t_r)=s_0$. ([[def-em-retarded-point-geometry]] (a)-(c))

[F2] Point-source history pairings: for the point-source distributions $\rho,J$ attached to $q$ and $z$, the retarded-history pairings $\Phi,\Upsilon$ define distributions on $\Omega$, are finite for every test, and satisfy $\langle\Phi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}C\psi/(\kappa r)$ and $\langle\Upsilon,\psi\rangle=\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}(\beta/c)C\psi/(\kappa r)$ componentwise; consequently $\varphi=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A=\beta\varphi/c$ are $C^2$ functions off the worldline whose locally integrable zero extensions have $\Phi,\Upsilon$ as their regular distributions. ([[lem-em-point-retarded-potential-and-fields]] (b))

[F3] Exact fields: with $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, one has $E=E_{\mathrm{vel}}+E_{\mathrm{acc}}$ with the displayed velocity and acceleration parts, $B=n\times E/c$, both fields $C^1$ off the worldline, and $|E_{\mathrm{vel}}|\le|C|(1+v_*/c)(1-v_*/c)^{-3}r^{-2}$. ([[thm-em-retarded-root-and-fields]] (c))

[F5] Distributional point-source Maxwell theorem: $W\Phi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $W\Upsilon=\mu_0J$ and $\operatorname{div}\Upsilon+c^{-2}\partial_t\Phi=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$; the distributions $\mathcal E=-\nabla\Phi-\partial_t\Upsilon$, $\mathcal B=\operatorname{curl}\Upsilon$ satisfy the four distributional Maxwell identities with the point pair; and off $\Gamma$ they restrict to the exact $C^1$ fields of [F3], the locally integrable zero extensions of the field formulas being their regular representatives. ([[thm-em-retarded-point-distributional-maxwell]] (a)-(c))

[F6] Weak source class and solution predicate: the all-time $C^3$ uniformly subluminal worldline with its proper graph is an admitted point source, the predicate consists of the four vanishing distributional pairings with the source pairings of the declared point class, and no product of two distributions is formed anywhere. ([[def-em-weak-sources]] (b),(e),(f))

[F7] Adopted singular-source physics: point-source models satisfying the weak predicate are the adopted physical models of the separate postulate, which the earlier smooth-source postulate neither covers nor implies. ([[post-em-distributional-vacuum-maxwell]])

[F8] Adopted selection: the retarded branch with no free addition is the framework's selected branch, and for the point-source branch the same selection is adopted in the weak equations of the singular-source model. ([[post-em-radiation-selection]] (b),(c))

[F9] Conventions: $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\nabla\times A$ are those of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]] with field classes of [[def-em-fields]]; $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$ are the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the curve $s\mapsto(z(s),s)$ is the laboratory reading of a prescribed massive future timelike worldline by [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]]. ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]])

[F11] Local Poynting balance: for jointly $C^1$ fields solving the smooth source-free vacuum Maxwell equations on a region, the local identity $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J\cdot E$ of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] holds there, and on a product neighborhood disjoint from $\Gamma$ the point pair restricts to zero. ([[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] (a),(c))

**Proof technique:** direct identification; clauses (a)-(d) instantiate the retarded point-geometry datum and the two point-source suppliers, and clause (e) instantiates the distributional point-source theorem and the weak solution predicate, with the physical adoption supplied separately by the postulates.

1.1 Potentials (a). By [F1] the root and retarded data $s,r,n,\beta,\kappa$ are defined and $C^3$-regular on $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$ with $\kappa\ge1-v_*/c>0$, and $C=q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$ is the stated signed constant [F9]. Clause (b) of [F2] identifies the retarded-history pairings with the exact integrals $\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}C\psi/(\kappa r)$ and $\int_{\Omega\setminus\Gamma}(\beta/c)C\psi/(\kappa r)$, and states that the potentials are the $C^2$ functions $\varphi=C/(\kappa r)$ and $A=\beta\varphi/c$ off the worldline whose zero extensions to $\Gamma$ are locally integrable. This is (a). [F1, F2, F9, algebra]

2.1 Exact fields (b). Clause (c) of [F3] gives, at every event of $\Omega\setminus\Gamma$, the split $E=E_{\mathrm{vel}}+E_{\mathrm{acc}}$ with the displayed velocity and acceleration parts, the relation $B=n\times E/c$, the $C^1$ regularity of both fields, and the velocity bound $|E_{\mathrm{vel}}|\le|C|(1+v_*/c)(1-v_*/c)^{-3}r^{-2}$; the fields are defined as $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ with the conventions of [F9], and the constant $C$ is retained with its sign in the field formulas while the bound uses $|C|$. This is (b). [step 1.1, F3, F9, algebra]

4.1 Constructed weak solution (e) and conclusion. By [F5](a) the potential distributions of [F2] satisfy $W\Phi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $W\Upsilon=\mu_0J$ and the distributional Lorenz identity, and by [F5](b) the field distributions $\mathcal E,\mathcal B$ satisfy all four distributional Maxwell identities with the point pair $\rho,J$; [F5](c) identifies their representatives with the locally integrable zero extensions of the off-worldline fields of [F3] and records that the off-worldline $C^1$ fields satisfy the source-free classical Maxwell equations. The all-time $C^3$ uniformly subluminal worldline with its proper graph is an admitted point source of the declared class [F6], the source pairings are those of the predicate, and the volume source parts vanish; hence the four identities are exactly the solution predicate of [F6](e) with $(\rho,J)$, and by the explicit physical adoption [F7] under the same retarded selection [F8] these constructed weak fields are the model fields of the point charge. This is the solution property claimed in (e); it is supplied by the mathematical theorem and not by the selection postulate. No product of distributions is formed anywhere ([F6](f)), and the zero extension on the null graph gives no physically defined self-field there. Finally, on a product neighborhood disjoint from $\Gamma$ the point pair restricts to the zero source so that the smooth source-free Maxwell equations of [F5](c) hold and the local Poynting identity [F11] applies there with $\rho=J=0$; it is never applied across the point source and forms no self-work or global finite-energy identity. This completes (e) and, with steps 1.1-3.1, all clauses (a)-(e). [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, F5, F6, F7, F8, F11, algebra] ∎

every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$, all derivatives being

[F3] The divergence is the sum of the three coordinate partial derivatives of
partial derivatives; only first partial derivatives occur.
[F4] The partial derivative $\partial_\mu F(a)$ is the derivative at $0$ of
([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]])

scalar multiples of the derivatives.

$\lambda f$ of maps $A\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous at a point are continuous at
that point; for $m=1$ this yields continuity of finite sums of continuous real
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]])
[F9] The distribution pairing is bilinear, and the distributional derivative
so it is linear in $u$. ([[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]])
**Proof technique:** direct; the smooth branch and the weak branch are computed separately.

1.1 Assume first that all pairs lie in the smooth branch. For jointly $C^1$ maps $F_1,\dots,F_n$ from the open set $\Omega\times I$ to $\mathbb R^q$ and scalars $a_1,\dots,a_n$, the combination $F:=\sum_ja_jF_j$ is jointly $C^1$ and $\partial_\mu F=\sum_ja_j\partial_\mu F_j$ for every coordinate index $\mu$: componentwise, at a point $a$ the line map $t\mapsto F^i(a+te_\mu)=\sum_ja_jF^i_j(a+te_\mu)$ is a finite sum of one-variable functions differentiable at $0$, so its derivative at $0$ exists and equals the combination $\sum_ja_j\partial_\mu F^i_j(a)$ of derivatives by [F5] through the line-map definition [F4], and each partial $\partial_\mu F^i=\sum_ja_j\partial_\mu F^i_j$ is continuous by the finite-sum clause [F6]; Hence $E$ and $B$ are jointly $C^1$ (and every additional derivative required by the branch combines by the same argument), while $\rho$ and $J$ are continuous by [F6]; thus all four combinations meet the regularity hypotheses of the smooth branch without assuming differentiability of the continuous sources. [F4, F5, F6]

1.2 Assume instead that all pairs lie in the weak branch. For locally integrable scalar fields $f_1,\dots,f_n$ on $I\times\Omega$ the combination $f:=\sum_ja_jf_j$ is locally integrable: on each compact $K\subseteq I\times\Omega$ the restrictions of the $f_j$ are $L^1$ functions on $K$, so their finite linear combination is $L^1$ on $K$ by [F7] and $\int_K|f|<\infty$. By the linearity in $f$ of the regular functional [F8] one has $u_f=\sum_ja_ju_{f_j}$, and by the defining formula and the bilinearity of the pairing [F9] the distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha u_f=\sum_ja_j\partial^\alpha u_{f_j}$, so that $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ of the combination are the corresponding combinations of the summands' distributional derivatives; componentwise the same holds for the vector fields $E_j$, $B_j$, $J_j$ and the scalar fields $\rho_j$. [F7, F8, F9]

2.1 The operators $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are linear on jointly $C^1$ vector fields: by the component formulas [F3] together with step 1.1, $\operatorname{div}(\sum_ja_jF_j)=\sum_i\partial_i(\sum_ja_jF^i_j)=\sum_ja_j\sum_i\partial_iF^i_j=\sum_ja_j\operatorname{div}F_j$, and the same finite rearrangement applied to the two-term difference in each curl component gives $\operatorname{curl}(\sum_ja_jF_j)=\sum_ja_j\operatorname{curl}F_j$; the same argument gives $\partial_t(\sum_ja_jF_j)=\sum_ja_j\partial_tF_j$. [step 1.1, F3]

2.2 In the weak branch, for each $\psi\in C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$, step 1.2 expands every pairing of the combination into the finite sum of the corresponding pairings of the summands, for instance $\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle=\sum_ja_j\langle\operatorname{div}E_j-\rho_j/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle$, and likewise for $\langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle$, $\langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle$ and $\langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$; since each summand pairing vanishes by [F2], all four pairings of the combination vanish, so the combination satisfies the branch in the distributional sense, which is clause (a) in that branch. [step 1.2, F2]

3.1 In the smooth branch, applying step 2.1 to the combinations $E=\sum_ja_jE_j$, $B=\sum_ja_jB_j$, $\rho=\sum_ja_j\rho_j$ and $J=\sum_ja_jJ_j$, and using [F1] for each summand, gives $\operatorname{div}E=\sum_ja_j\rho_j/\varepsilon_0=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{div}B=\sum_ja_j\cdot0=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\sum_ja_j\partial_tB_j=-\partial_tB$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\sum_ja_j(\mu_0J_j+c^{-2}\partial_tE_j)=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$, while step 1.1 supplies the regularity hypotheses; thus the combination satisfies the branch pointwise, which is clause (a) in that branch. [step 2.1, F1]
