regularity_scope_evidence: Let $c>0$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, and let $(\varphi,A)$ be a potential pair of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ in the restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]): for open $I$ this is the ordinary open-domain class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for non-open $I$ the pair is the restriction of a $C^2$ pair on an open neighbourhood of $\Omega\times I$, with relative derivatives at included endpoints and no time jet beyond the restricted values. Write $(E,B)$ for the field pair of $(\varphi,A)$ ([[def-em-fields]]) and
$$G:=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,\qquad W:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$$

for the Lorenz divergence and the wave expression of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. Let $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous source fields of the framework ([[def-em-sources]]).
$$\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+\nabla G\qquad\text{on }\Omega\times I.$$
with $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ the constant of that postulate.

(b) [Gauge shift] If $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ is a gauge function of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ ([[def-em-gauge-transformation]]), then $G(T_\chi(\varphi,A))=G-W\chi$ on $\Omega\times I$ and the transformed pair has the same field pair $(E,B)$ ([[pthm-em-gauge-invariance]]); hence $T_\chi(\varphi,A)$ is in Lorenz gauge if and only if $W\chi=G$ on $\Omega\times I$.

The two source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ hold automatically for every potential pair of class $C^2$. For an arbitrary given potential pair, the conjunction of Lorenz gauge with these two wave equations implies the sourced Maxwell system, but Maxwell's equations alone do not impose $G=0$ on that representative: their exact equivalent conditions remain the residual equations of (a), whose right-hand sides retain $\partial_tG$ and $\nabla G$.

(e) [Scope] The identities and equivalences are properties of the given $C^2$ representation. No gauge function with $W\chi=G$, and no generator meeting prescribed initial or boundary values, is asserted to exist; that is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses, treated by the gauge-reachability theorem later on this page. No boundary, decay or initial condition on the pair is imposed, and no empirical claim or observability of $\varphi$ or $A$ is included. A pair of class $C^1$ defines $E$, $B$ and $G$ but need not possess the second derivatives appearing in $W\varphi$, $WA$, $\Delta$ or $\partial_tG$, so $C^2$ is the exact standing regularity here.

**Given:** A constant $c>0$, an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^2$ jointly on $\Omega\times I$ in the restriction convention, its field pair $(E,B)$, the functions $G$ and $W$ displayed in the Statement, and continuous source fields $\rho,J$.

[F1] Potential-pair vocabulary: for a pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^m$, $m\ge1$, on an open set the electric and magnetic fields are $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ and are of class $C^{m-1}$; the Lorenz divergence is $G=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$, of class $C^{m-1}$; for $k\ge2$ the gauge transform of a class $C^k$ pair by a class $C^k$ function is $T_\chi(\varphi,A)=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi)$, of class $C^{k-1}$; the wave expression is $Wu=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u$ for class $C^2$ scalar and componentwise vector arguments; a pair is in Lorenz gauge when $G=0$; the definition asserts no existence or solvability ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]).

[F2] Restriction convention for a possibly non-open time interval: joint $C^m$ regularity on $\Omega\times I$ means restriction of a $C^m$ map on an open neighbourhood of $\Omega\times I$ in $\mathbb R^4$, spatial identities hold at every point of $\Omega\times I$ and time derivatives at included endpoints are the relative one-sided derivatives of the restriction; for open $I$ this is the ordinary class ([[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]]).

[F3] Framework vocabulary: $E$ and $B$ are the fixed-time spatial fields of the framework with the stated regularity and the polar/axial convention ([[def-em-fields]]); a smooth source field $(\rho,J)$ consists of maps continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates them ([[def-em-sources]]).

[F4] Linearity and algebra of derivatives: for $C^1$ fields $F,H$ on an open set and reals $\alpha,\beta$, $\operatorname{div}(\alpha F+\beta H)=\alpha\operatorname{div}F+\beta\operatorname{div}H$ and $\operatorname{curl}(\alpha F+\beta H)=\alpha\operatorname{curl}F+\beta\operatorname{curl}H$; partial derivatives are one-variable derivatives along coordinate lines and obey the sum and product rules componentwise ([[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F5] Clairaut--Schwarz: mixed coordinate partial derivatives of a $C^2$ function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$ commute, so for the jointly $C^2$ functions $\varphi$, $A$ and $\chi$ the identities $\partial_t\partial_i=\partial_i\partial_t$ hold componentwise and $\partial_i\partial_j=\partial_j\partial_i$ ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]).

[F6] Vector identity and Laplacian: for a $C^2$ field $F$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F$, and $\Delta F$ is the componentwise Laplacian defined by $\Delta f=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_i\partial_i\partial_if$ ([[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]], [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]).

[F7] Automatic source-free identities: for a $C^2$ field $F$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ one has $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}F=0$, and for a $C^2$ scalar $f$ one has $\operatorname{curl}\nabla f=0$ ([[thm-the-divergence-of-a-curl-vanishes]], [[thm-the-curl-of-a-gradient-vanishes]]).

[F2] The Laplacian is $\Delta F=(\Delta F_1,\Delta F_2,\Delta F_3)$ componentwise, and $\Delta f=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_i\partial_i\partial_if$ for $C^2$ scalars ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]); divergence and curl are the coordinate expressions $\operatorname{div}G=\sum_i\partial_iG_i$ and $\operatorname{curl}G=(\partial_2G_3-\partial_3G_2,\ \partial_3G_1-\partial_1G_3,\ \partial_1G_2-\partial_2G_1)$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]), with partial derivatives as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].
[F3] For a $C^2$ field $G$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$, $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}G)=0$ ([[thm-the-divergence-of-a-curl-vanishes]]).
[F4] For a $C^2$ field $G$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}G=\nabla\operatorname{div}G-\Delta G$ ([[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]]).

[F5] The compact smooth current class is the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b): $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero; the magnetostatic pair $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ is the time-independent reduction of clause (a) there, and the adopted smooth equations with these constants are [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]](a).
**Proof technique:** direct; componentwise reduction to the smooth Newtonian upgrade and the standard second-derivative vector identities.

1.1 For each $i$ the datum $J_i$ is smooth and compactly supported, so [F1] gives $A_i=\mu_0N(J_i)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, the derivative identity $D^\alpha A_i=\mu_0N(D^\alpha J_i)$ for every multi-index $\alpha$, and $-\Delta A_i=\mu_0J_i$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$; since all components are smooth, $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ by [F2], and $-\Delta A=\mu_0J$ holds pointwise componentwise. This is (a). [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Taking $\alpha=e_i$ in the derivative identity of step 1.1 and summing, $\operatorname{div}A=\sum_i\partial_iA_i=\mu_0\sum_iN(\partial_iJ_i)$; $N$ is componentwise linear by finite additivity of the integral over the compactly supported data, so this equals $\mu_0N(\sum_i\partial_iJ_i)=\mu_0N(\operatorname{div}J)$ pointwise, and $\operatorname{div}J=0$ gives $\operatorname{div}A=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$. This is (b), and the hypothesis $\operatorname{div}J=0$ is used in no other step. [step 1.1, F2, F5]

3.1 Since $A$ is $C^\infty$, the field $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ is $C^\infty$ by [F2]. Then $\operatorname{div}B=\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}A=0$ by [F3], and $\operatorname{curl}B=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}A=\nabla(\operatorname{div}A)-\Delta A$ by [F4]; substituting step 2.1 and step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{curl}B=0-(-\mu_0J)=\mu_0J$. Hence the magnetostatic pair of [F5] holds pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F2, F3, F4, F5]

4.1 Read step 3.1 inside the framework: [F5] identifies the pair $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ with the time-independent reduction of the adopted equations, and the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]](a) then holds for the fields $E:=0$, $\rho:=0$ on $\Omega\times I$ and the time-independent $B,J$ restricted to $\Omega\times I$: indeed $\operatorname{div}E=0=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ and $\partial_tB=0$ give $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, and $\partial_tE=0$ with $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ gives $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. More generally a compatible steady electrostatic pair satisfying $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ and $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ may be combined with $B,J$; no existence theorem for such a pair is asserted here. [step 3.1, F5]

Griffiths, Section 5.4.1, printed pp. 234-240, derives the Poisson equation $\nabla^2A=-\mu_0J$ in the Coulomb gauge and gives the integral solution (5.63); Tong, Sections 3.2-3.2.3, printed pp. 46-52, and Chew, Lecture 4 Section 4.1, printed pp. 39-41, give the same componentwise construction; Landau-Lifshitz, Section 43, printed pp. 101-103, gives the corresponding constant-field formulation in Gaussian units, re-expressed here in SI. The proof above is the exact componentwise version: smoothness and the Poisson identity come from the smooth Newtonian upgrade, and the divergence-free hypothesis enters only through step 2.1.

regularity_scope_evidence: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis under which [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] and the surface conventions of [[def-em-weak-sources]] are stated, and let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]].

Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), let $\sigma_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $K_f(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a free surface charge density and a tangential free surface current density, both stationary in $t$), and let $\rho_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous and locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$. Let $E,B,D,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$, with the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension property: around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side of each field is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder, so that the fields and their first space and time derivatives extend continuously to that side, locally uniformly on compact cylinders. Write $[F]=F_+-F_-$ for the jump of the one-sided traces.

**[Thin-interface hypothesis]** Suppose that $E,B,D,H$ satisfy the four macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] in the distributional sense on $U$ with the source pair $\rho_f=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$, $J_f=J_v+K_f\delta_S$, where the stationary-sheet pairings are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) and the equations are $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ as identities in the sense of [[def-distribution]], the fields being identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\psi$ ranging over $C_c^\infty(U)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). This thin-interface solution hypothesis is a modelling assumption of the statement: it is the natural weakening of the smooth macroscopic equations to fields with a common stationary discontinuity, and it is not deduced from the smooth-region equations alone.

**[Weak-trace branch]** If instead of the joint extension hypothesis the fields have the original one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time and, in addition, the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the one-sided field traces are measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ with respect to $dS\,dt$, then the same four identities hold as identities of sheet distributions and for $dS\,dt$-almost every $(x,t)$; since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, they hold for every $x\in S$ for almost every $t$, and at every $(x,t)$ whenever the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous. Merely having one-sided spatial $C^1$ traces separately at every time does not justify the last upgrade.

**[Scope]** In the joint one-sided spacetime $C^1$ extension branch, stationarity and the joint extensions make $\partial_tD$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally integrable, contributing no delta terms. In the weak-trace branch the explicitly assumed locally integrable temporal derivatives provide this conclusion instead. No magnetic charge and no magnetic surface current are present in the sources; no dipolar sheet layer (a concentrated dipole distribution in $P$ or $M$, which would make the fields non-integrable) is included. No existence theorem for fields with singular sources is asserted, no constitutive law is used, and no empirical claim is made.

**Given:** The objects and hypotheses of the Statement, with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the operators and constant conventions of the Statement; and the thin-interface hypothesis [A1]. The fields $E,B,D,H$ are identified with their regular distributions, and the source pair with the stationary-sheet pairings of [A1].

[A1] The thin-interface hypothesis: the four identities $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_v+K_f\delta_S+\partial_tD$ hold as distributions on $U$, with the source pair of the stationary-sheet pairings and the equation forms of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]. This solution hypothesis is assumed, not deduced.

[L1] For a two-sided compact embedded $C^2$ interface $S$ with unit normal $n$ from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$ and a field $F$ that is $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided $C^1$ traces, $\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}+n\cdot[F]\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}+n\times[F]\delta_S$, where $\{\cdot\}$ denotes the piecewise classical field and $[F]=F_+-F_-$ ([[lem-em-interface-derivatives]]).

[L2] The surface convention: $\delta_S(\psi)=\int_S\psi\,dS$ for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with $dS$ the surface measure of the compact embedded hypersurface; a continuous density $a$ on $S$ defines $a\delta_S(\psi)=\int_S a\psi\,dS$, both functionals of finite order ([[def-em-surface-distribution]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

[L3] The chart integral defines a finite Borel measure on the compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, independent of the finite regular charts; every regular chart density $J_X$ is continuous and strictly positive ([[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

[L4] Locally integrable fields embed as regular distributions by $u_f(\psi)=\int_U f\psi$, and the embedding is injective modulo almost-everywhere equality under Countable Choice ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

[L5] The image of a $C^1$ map from a lower-dimensional smooth manifold into a higher-dimensional one is a null subset ([[prop-the-image-of-a-lower-dimensional-c1-manifold-is-null]]), and a countable union of null sets is null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]).

[L6] For compact $K$ in an open set there are smooth compactly supported cutoffs equal to one near $K$ ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]); if $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere with $|f_n|\le g$ for a single integrable $g$, then $\int f_n\to\int f$ ([[thm-dominated-convergence]]); the coordinate hyperplane $\{x_3=0\}$ in $\mathbb R^4$ is Lebesgue-null as the graph of a measurable function ([[cor-graph-of-a-measurable-function-is-lebesgue-null]]).

[L7] If $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega')$ on an open $\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ satisfies $\int g\varphi=0$ for every test function $\varphi$, then $g=0$ almost everywhere ([[lem-fundamental-lemma-of-the-calculus-of-variations]]); locally a $C^1$ domain boundary is, after a rigid change of coordinates, the graph of a $C^1$ function, with the domain on one side ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]).

[L8] For $C^1$ functions on a closed interval, one-dimensional integration by parts holds ([[thm-integration-by-parts]]); for $L^1$ functions on sigma-finite product spaces the iterated and multiple integrals agree ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**Proof technique:** first test away from the interface to remove the locally integrable volume part, then extract the continuous coefficient with the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations in surface charts.

1.1 The surface $S$ is Lebesgue-null in $\Omega$: by [L3] the finitely many regular charts $X_j:V_j\to S$ cover $S$, each image $X_j(V_j)$ is null in $\mathbb R^3$ by [L5] because $X_j$ is a $C^1$ map from the lower-dimensional open set $V_j\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, and a finite union of null sets is null by [L5]. Consequently, for $F\in\{B,D\}$ the distributional time derivative of the regular distribution of $F$ is the regular distribution of the piecewise classical time derivative: fix a test $\psi$ with support in a compact cylinder $\overline Q\times J\subseteq U$, so that $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=-\int_U F\partial_t\psi$; by [L8] applied after Fubini, this iterated integral equals $-\int_Q\int_JF(x,t)\partial_t\psi(x,t)\,dt\,dx$, and for every $x\in\Omega\setminus S$ the inner integrand is $C^1$ in $t$ with $\psi(x,\cdot)$ compactly supported in $J$, so [L8] gives $\int_JF(x,t)\partial_t\psi(x,t)\,dt=-\int_J\partial_tF(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dt$; since $S$ is null, replacing the outer integral over $\Omega\setminus S$ by one over $\Omega$ changes nothing, so $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=\int_U\{\partial_tF\}\psi$ for every test $\psi$, where $\{\partial_tF\}$ is locally bounded by the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension hypothesis. [L3, L5, L8]

1.2 By [L1], applied to $D$, $B$, $E$, $H$ (each is $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided $C^1$ traces under the joint extension hypothesis), the four spatial identities $\operatorname{div}D=\{\operatorname{div}D\}+n\cdot[D]\delta_S$, $\operatorname{div}B=\{\operatorname{div}B\}+n\cdot[B]\delta_S$, $\operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+n\times[E]\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}H=\{\operatorname{curl}H\}+n\times[H]\delta_S$ hold as distributions on $U$ under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, with the piecewise fields locally bounded near $S$. [L1]

2.1 [Coefficient extraction] Let $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and let $a$ be measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ for $dS\,dt$, with $u_g+a\delta_S=0$. Every smooth test supported away from $S\times I$ has zero sheet pairing; the fundamental lemma [L7] applied on that open complement therefore gives $g=0$ almost everywhere there. Since $S$ is null by step 1.1, Fubini [L8] makes $S\times I$ null locally in spacetime, so $g=0$ almost everywhere on $U$. Thus $\int_{S\times I}a\psi\,dS\,dt=0$ for every ambient smooth compact test $\psi$. In a sufficiently small rigid graph chart write $X(y)=(y,h(y))$, with a product box $V\times(z_-,z_+)\times J$ contained in the ambient chart/time domain. Shrink $V$ and the height interval so the graph over $V$ stays in a closed subinterval inside $(z_-,z_+)$. For any $\eta\in C_c^\infty(V\times J)$ choose $\beta\in C_c^\infty((z_-,z_+))$ equal to $1$ on that graph-height interval by [L6], and take the ambient smooth test $\psi(y,z,t)=\eta(y,t)\beta(z)$, transported by the rigid motion and extended by zero. This test uses no composition with the merely $C^2$ graph function; its restriction to $S$ is $\eta$. The chart formula [L3] gives $\int_{V\times J}(a\circ X)(y,t)J_X(y)\eta(y,t)\,dy\,dt=0$. By [L7], $(a\circ X)J_X=0$ almost everywhere; positivity and continuity of $J_X$ give $a=0$ surface-time almost everywhere. Such small boxes cover every chart, so the conclusion holds on $S\times I$. In the joint branch $a\circ X$ is continuous; if it were nonzero at one point it would stay bounded away from zero on a nonempty parameter-time box of positive Lebesgue measure, contradicting the almost-everywhere conclusion. Thus $a=0$ pointwise in that branch. [step 1.1, L2, L3, L6, L7, L8]

2.2 Substituting the spatial identities of step 1.2 and the temporal identity of step 1.1 into the assumed identities [A1] gives four distributional identities of the form $u_g+a\delta_S=0$ with locally integrable volume parts: $u_{\{\operatorname{div}D\}-\rho_v}+(n\cdot[D]-\sigma_f)\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{div}B\}}+n\cdot[B]\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+\{\partial_tB\}}+n\times[E]\delta_S=0$ and $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}H\}-J_v-\{\partial_tD\}}+(n\times[H]-K_f)\delta_S=0$; the sums are locally integrable because the piecewise fields and $J_v,\rho_v$ are locally integrable and the piecewise derivatives are locally bounded near $S$ (joint branch) or assumed locally integrable (weak-trace branch), and the sheet coefficients are the stated one-sided jump densities, continuous in the joint branch. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, L2, L4]

3.1 Apply step 2.1 to each of the four identities of step 2.2: the four coefficients $n\cdot[D]-\sigma_f$, $n\cdot[B]$, $n\times[E]$ and $n\times[H]-K_f$ vanish $dS\,dt$-almost everywhere, and in the joint branch they are continuous on $S\times I$ (one-sided traces of locally uniformly continuous extensions), hence vanish pointwise on $S\times I$; this proves $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$, $n\cdot[B]=0$, $n\times[E]=0$ and $n\times[H]=K_f$ pointwise, equivalently $\sigma_f=n\cdot[D]$ and $K_f=n\times[H]$, and the inner and cross products are those of the one-sided traces written in the frame basis of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. In the weak-trace branch the four coefficients vanish $dS\,dt$-almost everywhere; since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, vanishing on a set of full $dS$-measure for almost every $t$ upgrades to every $x\in S$ for almost every $t$, and if the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous, to every $(x,t)\in S\times I$; the four identities hold as identities of sheet distributions in both branches, and all statements are conditional on the assumed distributional equations [A1] with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ carried from step 1.2. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, A1, L1, L2, L5] ∎

5.1 [Brewster condition, part (c)] In each finite-admittance branch the formula of step 3.1 gives $r_\chi=0$ exactly when the numerator $Y^\chi_1-Y^\chi_2$ vanishes, i.e. $Y^\chi_1=Y^\chi_2$. Assume now $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu$ and $|\kappa|<K_2$, so that the (p) admittances are real positive. The condition $Y^p_1=Y^p_2$ reads $\varepsilon_1/k_{13}=\varepsilon_2/k_{t3}$; substituting $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$ and $k_{j3}=(\omega n_j/c)\cos\theta_j$ (from $k_{13}=K_1\cos\theta_i=(\omega n_1/c)\cos\theta_i$ and $k_{t3}=K_2\cos\theta_t=(\omega n_2/c)\cos\theta_t$) gives $n_1\cos\theta_t=n_2\cos\theta_i$. Together with Snell's law $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$ of step 4.1, squaring both and eliminating $\sin^2\theta_t$ gives $(n_1^2-n_2^2)\bigl[n_2^2-(n_1^2+n_2^2)\sin^2\theta_i\bigr]=0$: indeed $n_1^2(1-\sin^2\theta_t)=n_2^2\cos^2\theta_i$ and $\sin\theta_t=(n_1/n_2)\sin\theta_i$ yield $n_1^2n_2^2-n_1^4\sin^2\theta_i=n_2^4-n_2^4\sin^2\theta_i$, i.e. $n_2^2(n_1^2-n_2^2)=(n_1^2-n_2^2)(n_1^2+n_2^2)\sin^2\theta_i$. If $n_1\ne n_2$, division by the nonzero first factor gives $\sin^2\theta_i=n_2^2/(n_1^2+n_2^2)$; since $0<\theta_i<\pi/2$ and sine is strictly increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ with $\sin 0=0$ by [F8], this determines the unique admissible angle $\theta_B:=\arcsin\bigl(n_2/\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}\bigr)\in(0,\pi/2)$, at which $r_p=0$ by construction. At this angle $\cos\theta_B>0$: cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ by [F8], so $0<\theta_B<\pi/2$ gives $\cos\theta_B>\cos(\pi/2)=0$. The Pythagorean identity of [F8] then gives $\cos\theta_B=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta_B}=n_1/\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}$, so $\tan\theta_B=\sin\theta_B/\cos\theta_B=n_2/n_1$ by the definition of tangent in [F8]; no other admissible angle has this tangent, because tangent is strictly increasing on $(0,\pi/2)$ by [F8]. If instead $n_1=n_2$ and $\mu_1=\mu_2$ then $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ and the two media are identical: $k_{13}=k_{t3}$ and $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ give $Y^\chi_1=Y^\chi_2$, so $r_s=r_p=0$ and $t_s=t_p=1$ at every admissible angle (where the (p) formula applies), with no distinguished Brewster angle. 1.1 (Clause (a): laboratory components of $e$ and $b$) By [F2], $n^0=\gamma_w$ and $n^i=\gamma_w w_i/c$, so with the dictionary [F1] the covariant components are $e_0=F_{00}n^0+F_{0i}n^i=-(\gamma_w/c^2)E\cdot w$ and $e_i=F_{i0}n^0+F_{ij}n^j=\frac{\gamma_w}{c}E_i+\frac{\gamma_w}{c}\epsilon_{ijk}w_jB_k=\frac{\gamma_w}{c}\bigl(E_i+(w\times B)_i\bigr)$, using $F_{i0}=-F_{0i}=E_i/c$ and $(w\times B)_i=\epsilon_{ijk}w_jB_k$ [F1]. For the dual, the definition $(*F)_{ab}=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$ and the components of [F1] give $(*F)_{0i}=B_i$ and $(*F)_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}E_k/c$: indeed $\varepsilon_{0i}{}^{jk}=\varepsilon_{0ijk}=\epsilon_{ijk}$ because raising the two spatial indices is free and $(0,i,j,k)$ is an even permutation of $(0,1,2,3)$ exactly when $(i,j,k)$ is even, so $(*F)_{0i}=\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}=\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{jk\ell}B_\ell=B_i$ with $\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{jk\ell}=2\delta_{i\ell}$ (direct enumeration); and $\varepsilon_{ij}{}^{0k}=\eta^{00}\eta^{kk}\varepsilon_{ij0k}=-\varepsilon_{ij0k}=-\epsilon_{ijk}$, since $(0,i,j,k)\mapsto(i,j,0,k)$ is an even permutation, so $(*F)_{ij}=\varepsilon_{ij}{}^{0k}F_{0k}=(-\epsilon_{ijk})(-E_k/c)=\epsilon_{ijk}E_k/c$. Hence $b_0=(*F)_{00}n^0+(*F)_{0i}n^i=\frac{\gamma_w}{c}B\cdot w$ and $b_i=(*F)_{i0}n^0+(*F)_{ij}n^j=-\gamma_wB_i+\frac{\gamma_w}{c^2}\epsilon_{ijk}w_jE_k=-\gamma_w\bigl(B_i-\frac{(w\times E)_i}{c^2}\bigr)$. These are the four displayed component formulas of clause (a); in particular the laboratory temporal components $e_0,b_0$ need not vanish, so the orthogonality of the decomposition cannot be read as the vanishing of these laboratory components. 1.3 (Clause (a): the observer's inertial rest frame and the observed components) At $w=0$, $B(0)$ is the identity and $n=e_0$, so the rest frame is the laboratory frame and the displayed identity is immediate without a division by $|w/c|^2$. For $w\ne0$, applying the matrix of [F3] to the vector $n=\gamma_w(1,w/c)$ of [F2] gives $\bigl(B(w/c)n\bigr)^0=\gamma_w\bigl(\gamma_w-\frac{w}{c}\cdot\frac{\gamma_w w}{c}\bigr)=\gamma_w^2(1-|w|^2/c^2)=1$ and $\bigl(B(w/c)n\bigr)_{\mathrm{vec}}=\frac{\gamma_w w}{c}+\frac{\gamma_w-1}{|w/c|^2}\Bigl(\frac{w}{c}\cdot\frac{\gamma_w w}{c}\Bigr)\frac{w}{c}-\gamma_w\frac{w}{c}\gamma_w=\gamma_w\frac{w}{c}\bigl[1+(\gamma_w-1)-\gamma_w\bigr]=0$; hence $n$ has coordinates $(1,0,0,0)$ in the chart $x'=B(w/c)x+b$, that is $n=e'_0$: the chart $x'$ is the observer's inertial rest frame, and it is an admissible inertial change of description because $B(w/c)$ is proper orthochronous [F3]. By clause (a′) of [F3] the components of the same $F$ read in $x'$ are the boosted components with vector parameter $v=w$: $E'_\parallel=E_\parallel$, $B'_\parallel=B_\parallel$, $E'_\perp=\gamma_w(E+w\times B)_\perp$ and $B'_\perp=\gamma_w(B-w\times E/c^2)_\perp$ along $\widehat w$, with the displayed closed formulas, and $E'=E$, $B'=B$ when $w=0$. Reading the dictionary [F1] in the rest frame with $n=e'_0$ gives $e'_0=b'_0=0$, $e'_i=F'_{i0}=-F'_{0i}=E'_i/c$ and $b'_i=(*F')_{i0}=-(*F')_{0i}=-B'_i$; hence the vectors $E_n=c\,e^\sharp$ and $B_n=-b^\sharp$ have rest-frame components $(0,E')$ and $(0,B')$. 1.4 (Clause (b): the phase covector, nonzero, future and null) By [F4] the wavevector is $\mathbf k=Ks$ with $|\mathbf k|=K=\omega/c$ and propagation direction $\widehat{\mathbf k}=s$, and the phase is $\theta(x,t)=\mathbf k\cdot x-\omega t$. 2.1 [Divergence constraints in coefficient form] For $K:=(\pi m/a,\pi n/b,2\pi\xi)$ the distributionally zero divergence of the extended field is equivalent to $K\cdot\widehat E=K\cdot\widehat B=0$ for almost every $\xi$, and the finite-energy reflection class is exactly the class of coefficient families satisfying these almost-everywhere constraints together with the parities and $L^2$ summability. The derivative correspondence is proved on the dense test class of finite transverse-character sums times longitudinal Schwartz functions: for such a test $\psi$, finite transverse integration by parts and the exact identity $\mathcal F_2(\partial_z\psi)=2\pi i\xi\widehat\psi$ of [F3] turn the pairing $\int F\cdot\nabla\psi$ into the sum of the coefficient pairings against $iK\cdot\widehat F$, and the compactly supported smooth tests used in the definition are obtained by multiplying with cutoffs $\chi_R$ of [F3] and passing to the limit, since the tests and their first derivatives converge in $L^2$ and all pairings are bounded by Cauchy–Schwarz [F6]; conversely a test with $K\cdot\widehat F=0$ almost everywhere has zero weak divergence pairing, and the general compact smooth tests are reached through the transverse $L^2$ expansions of their derivatives and the Schwartz transform isomorphism [F3]. Hence the exact constrained class corresponds to the stated almost-everywhere coefficient constraints, not merely to a scalar basis without Gauss equations; for smooth fields the divergences vanish pointwise and the four-wall PEC conditions hold by the reading of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]]. reference_text: Assume the Axiom of Choice as carried by [[lem-em-exterior-vector-helmholtz-mixed-boundary-existence]], whose variational, Sobolev-compactness and compact-spectral steps use it; the algebraic computations below use no further choice. Let $O\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set with $C^\infty$ boundary, $D:=\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline O$ connected, $k>0$, $\omega:=ck$ with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and $R>0$ with $\overline O\subset B_R(0)$; let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open with $\overline D\subseteq V$, and let $(\widetilde E_{\rm inc},\widetilde B_{\rm inc})$ be a $C^\infty$ frequency-$\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pair on $V$ ([[def-em-monochromatic-source-free-phasors]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]). Plane-wave instances are provided by [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]: if $\kappa\cdot e=0$, $b=\kappa\times e/\omega$ and $|\kappa|=\omega/c$, then $(\widetilde E_{\rm inc},\widetilde B_{\rm inc})(x)=(e\,e^{i\kappa\cdot x},b\,e^{i\kappa\cdot x})$ satisfies the four phasor equations on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]). Adopt the ideal perfectly conducting (PEC) boundary model: the tangential component of the total electric field vanishes on $\partial O$. This is a declared idealization of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]] with vanishing fields inside the conductor; it is not one of the finite-conductivity branches of [[post-em-material-closure]], and the induced surface charge and current are neither prescribed nor determined here. Let $e_T$ be the tangential projection of $-\widetilde E_{\rm inc}$ on $\partial O$, and let $\widetilde E_{\rm scat}$ be the unique $C^\infty$ field on $\overline D$ of [[lem-em-exterior-vector-helmholtz-mixed-boundary-existence]] with $(\Delta+k^2)\widetilde E_{\rm scat}=0$ and $\operatorname{div}\widetilde E_{\rm scat}=0$ on $D$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]), tangential trace $e_T$ on $\partial O$ and that lemma's outgoing modal condition on $S_R$. Set $\widetilde B_{\rm scat}:=(i\omega)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E_{\rm scat}$ and, on $D$, $\widetilde E_{\rm tot}:=\widetilde E_{\rm inc}+\widetilde E_{\rm scat}$, $\widetilde B_{\rm tot}:=\widetilde B_{\rm inc}+\widetilde B_{\rm scat}$. Then: (a) [Phasor Maxwell] $(\widetilde E_{\rm scat},\widetilde B_{\rm scat})$ and $(\widetilde E_{\rm tot},\widetilde B_{\rm tot})$ are $C^\infty$ frequency-$\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pairs on $D$; and for every $C^\infty$ frequency-$\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pair $(\widetilde E,\widetilde B)$ on an open set $O'\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, the associated real fields of [[def-em-monochromatic-source-free-phasors]] satisfy on $O'\times\mathbb R$ the smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$ and $J\equiv0$. Consequently the associated real total fields $E_{\rm tot},B_{\rm tot}$ satisfy those source-free equations on $D\times\mathbb R$. (b) [PEC boundary condition] the tangential trace of $\widetilde E_{\rm tot}$ on $\partial O$ vanishes; hence for every unit normal field $n$ of $\partial O$ the associated real total electric field $E_{\rm tot}(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E_{\rm tot}(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) satisfies $n\times E_{\rm tot}=0$ on $\partial O\times\mathbb R$. 1.2 (Clause (a): the power identity) For the temporal index, [F2] and [F3] give $m\,dU^0/d\tau=q\,\Phi(U)^0=q\gamma E\cdot v/c$. By [F1] and [F5], $U^0=\gamma c$ and $dU^0/d\tau=\gamma c\,\mathrm d\gamma/\mathrm dt$, so $m\,dU^0/d\tau=\frac{\gamma}{c}\,mc^2\frac{\mathrm d\gamma}{\mathrm dt}=\frac{\gamma}{c}\frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}$; comparing with the right-hand side, $\frac{\gamma}{c}\frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}=\frac{q\gamma E\cdot v}{c}$, and multiplying by $c/\gamma>0$ gives $d(\gamma mc^2)/dt=q\,E\cdot v$. 1.3 (Clause (b): norm preservation and the future branch) Since $m\,dU/d\tau=q\,\Phi(U)$ with constant $m\ne0$ and $q$ and $F$ possibly varying along the trajectory, the norm-conservation clause of [F6] applies (it needs no derivative of $F$) and gives that $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on $J$; being the four-velocity of the massive worldline, $U$ has norm $-c^2$ at every point by [F1]. Thus $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ everywhere, and the component identity $(U^0)^2=c^2+|U_{\mathrm{vec}}|^2\ge c^2>0$ shows that $U^0$ never vanishes; $U^0$ is continuous because $U$ is differentiable [F6], so on every interval of $J$ it has constant sign by [F6]. If the initial data are future timelike, $U^0(0)>0$, so $U^0>0$ throughout, the solution remains in the future timelike branch, and $|v|^2/c^2=1-\gamma^{-2}<1$, that is $|v(t)|<c$, wherever the chart reading is differentiable. No existence or continuation of solutions is asserted. [given, F1, F2, F6, algebra]

1.4 (Clause (c): the function and its derivatives) Put $z(t):=|v(t)|^2/c^2$, so that $0\le z\le\delta^2$ on an interval where $|v|/c\le\delta$, $\delta\in(0,1)$, and $\gamma=f(z)$ with $f(z):=(1-z)^{-1/2}$. The function $f$ is continuous on $[0,\delta^2]$ and differentiable on $(0,\delta^2)$: it is the composition of $z\mapsto1-z$ with $y\mapsto y^{-1/2}$, the latter continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$ with derivative $-\tfrac12y^{-3/2}$ [F7], and $\gamma=f(z)$ agrees with the rational power of [F1] by [F7]. By the chain rule [F5], $f'(z)=\tfrac12(1-z)^{-3/2}$ and $f''(z)=\tfrac34(1-z)^{-5/2}$ on $(0,\delta^2)$. If $z=0$ then $\gamma=1$ and every difference and bound in clause (c) vanishes exactly; hence assume $0<z\le\delta^2$ below, and note $1-\delta^2>0$. [given, F1, F5, F7, algebra]

2.1 (Clause (c): first-order bound) Since $f$ is continuous on $[0,z]$ and differentiable on $(0,z)$, [F8] gives $\xi\in(0,z)$ with $f(z)-f(0)=f'(\xi)z$, and $f(0)=1$; hence $|\gamma-1|=|f'(\xi)|\,z=\tfrac12(1-\xi)^{-3/2}z$. Since $0<\xi\le z\le\delta^2<1$, the base satisfies $1-\xi\ge1-\delta^2>0$, so $0<(1-\xi)^{-3/2}\le(1-\delta^2)^{-3/2}$ by monotonicity of the positive power and positivity of inverses [F7]; therefore $|\gamma-1|\le\frac{z}{2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}=\frac{|v|^2/c^2}{2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}$. 2.2 (Clause (c): second-order bound) Define $q(s):=f(s)-1-\tfrac{s}{2}$ and $g(s):=s^2$ on $[0,z]$; both are continuous on $[0,z]$ and differentiable on $(0,z)$, with $q'(s)=f'(s)-\tfrac12$ and $g'(s)=2s>0$ there [F7, F8]. The mean value theorem [F8] applied to $f'$ on $[0,\xi]$, where $f'$ is continuous on $[0,\xi]$ and differentiable on $(0,\xi)$ (the derivative $f''$ is given on $(0,\delta^2)$ in step 1.4), gives $\eta\in(0,\xi)$ with $f'(\xi)-f'(0)=\xi f''(\eta)$; since $f'(0)=\tfrac12$ this gives $f'(\xi)-\tfrac12=\xi f''(\eta)$, and substitution yields $f(z)-1-\tfrac z2=\frac{z^2}{2\xi}\cdot\xi f''(\eta)=\tfrac12f''(\eta)z^2=\tfrac38(1-\eta)^{-5/2}z^2$. 4.1 (Clauses (c) and (d): status and scope) Clauses (a) and (b) are steps 1.1-1.3, and clause (c) is steps 1.4, 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1: the two first-order and second-order bounds, the resulting momentum and energy bounds and their uniformity in $|v|/c\le\delta$ are established there, including the exact vanishing at $z=0$. [F2] Gauge identities and the decoupling definition: for a potential pair of class $C^2$ jointly on an open set, $\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG$ and $\operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+\nabla G$ hold there, the source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ hold automatically for any potential pair, and if in addition $G=0$ then the sourced Maxwell system of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds if and only if $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $WA=\mu_0J$; the fields $E,B$, the Lorenz divergence $G$ and the wave expression $W$ are those of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]], and field regularity classes are those of [[def-em-fields]]. [F5] Source fields: smooth source fields $(\rho,J)$ with their units, the continuity equation and the compact-support convention are those of [[def-em-sources]]; the standing hypotheses of this theorem are as stated in the Given. ([[def-em-sources]])

[F6] $C^1$ change of variables for $L^1$: for a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $T:U\to V$ of open sets and $f\in L^1(\lambda_n)$, $\int_Vf=\int_U f\circ T\,|\det DT|$. ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]])

([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]])

[F12] $C^k$ means continuous partial derivatives up to order $k$; finite sums and products of $C^k$ maps are $C^k$. ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]])

[F14] For $C^2$ fields and $C^1$ sources satisfying the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]], the continuity equation is forced; here continuity is assumed for the prescribed source. ([[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] (a))

1.1 Smoothness and wave equations. The source pair $(\rho,J)$ is jointly $C^\infty$ and vanishes outside the compact set $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$, so $\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and each $h=\mu_0J_k$ belongs to $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$ [F5, F12]. Applying [F1] to these functions and using the identification $\varphi=\varepsilon_0^{-1}(K*\rho)$, $A_k=\mu_0(K*J_k)$ of the Given gives that $\varphi$ and every component of $A$ are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, with $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $WA=\mu_0J$ pointwise. This is (a). [F1, F4, F5, F12]

1.2 Derivative identities for the retarded kernel. Fix $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R)$. For fixed $(x,t)$ the change of variable $y\mapsto z=x-y$, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^3$ with $|\det D(x-\cdot)|=1$, is legitimate for the integrable function $y\mapsto h(y,t-|x-y|/c)/(4\pi|x-y|)$ [F6], so $(K*h)(x,t)=\int h(x-z,t-|z|/c)/(4\pi|z|)\,dz$. For a compact parameter block $|x|\le R$, $|t|\le R$ and any first partial derivative of $h$, the differentiated integrand $z\mapsto(\partial h)(x-z,t-|z|/c)/(4\pi|z|)$ (zero at $z=0$) is dominated by $M_R\mathbf 1_{B_{2R}}(z)/|z|$ with $M_R$ the supremum of the relevant derivative of $h$ on the compact set $\{|y|\le R+a+1,\ t\in[-R-1,R+1]\}$, because the numerator vanishes whenever $|x-z|>a$; that majorant is integrable by [F8] (in three dimensions $\int_{B_{2R}}|z|^{-1}dz=2\pi(2R)^2$). The derivative is measurable as a limit of measurable difference quotients, so [F7] applies once per parameter $x_1,x_2,x_3,t$ with the other three parameters held fixed, and gives $\partial_{x_i}(K*h)=K*(\partial_{y_i}h)$ and $\partial_t(K*h)=K*(\partial_th)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, where $\partial_{y_i}h$ is the partial derivative of $h$ in its $i$-th spatial argument. [F6, F7, F8]

1.4 Total charge. By the support hypothesis, $Q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho(y,t)dy=\int_{B_a(0)}\rho(y,t)dy$ for every $t$, and $Q(t)=0$ for $t<t_0$; the integral depends smoothly on $t$ with $Q'(t)=\int_{B_a(0)}\partial_t\rho(y,t)dy$ by [F11] applied to the fixed compact $B_a(0)$ (the integrands $\rho,\partial_t\rho$ are continuous on a neighbourhood of $\overline B_a(0)\times[t]$) [F5, F12]. Fix $t$ and $R>a$; the continuity equation and the divergence theorem [F10] give $\int_{B_a(0)}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=\int_{B_R(0)}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=\int_{\partial B_R(0)}J(y,t)\cdot\nu\,dS=0$, because $J$ vanishes outside $\overline B_a(0)$ and $R>a$; hence $Q'(t)=-\int_{B_a(0)}\operatorname{div}J(y,t)dy=0$. 2.2 Zero-data Cauchy identification. Fix $t_1<t_0$ and $T'>t_0$. By step 1.3, $\varphi(\cdot,t_1)=0$, $A(\cdot,t_1)=0$ and also $\partial_t\varphi(\cdot,t_1)=0$, $\partial_tA(\cdot,t_1)=0$ (the same vanishing argument applies to the time derivatives, whose integrands contain $\rho_t,J_t$, vanishing for retarded arguments $<t_0$ as well). By [F2] with the Lorenz divergence $G$ of step 2.1, $\operatorname{div}E=W\varphi-\partial_tG=\rho/\varepsilon_0-0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B-c^{-2}\partial_tE=WA+\nabla G=\mu_0J+0$; the two source-free equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ are automatic for the potential pair [F2]. Hence the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] holds for $(E,B,\rho,J)$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ with $E,B$ of class $C^\infty$, which is (c). [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, F2, F13, F14, algebra] ∎

reference_text: Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] and [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]] ([[def-countable-choice]]), whose trace qualification is used in clause (d); the full-Choice modal branch of the latter is not used. Adopt the scalar aperture model and its notation from [[post-em-scalar-aperture-model]]: frequency $\omega>0$, $k=\omega/c$, aperture radius $a>0$, finite complex aperture distribution $\alpha$ supported in the planar aperture $S\subset\{y_3=0\}\cap\{y:|y|\le a\}$, model field $u=G_k*\alpha$, real field $U(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(u(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and $T=2\pi/\omega$ ([[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]). Set $I(x):=(1/2)|u(x)|^2$. Then: (a) [Model field and Fraunhofer estimate] $u$ is $C^\infty$ on the half-space $\{x_3>0\}$ and on $\mathbb R^3\setminus S$, satisfies $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ there, and is outgoing in the sense of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]: for $x=rn$ with $r\ge2a$ and $n\in S^2$, $$u(rn)=\frac{e^{ikr}}{4\pi r}\int e^{-ikn\cdot y}\,d\alpha(y)+O\Bigl(\frac{\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}}{r}\Bigl[\frac ar+\frac{ka^2}{r}\Bigr]\Bigr)$$ uniformly in direction, and $r(\partial_ru-iku)=O(r^{-1})$ uniformly. (b) [Fresnel estimate] write $y_t=(y_1,y_2)$ and $\xi=(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ for transverse vectors; for the planar aperture and observation $x=(\xi_1,\xi_2,z)$ with $z>0$, $b\ge0$, $|\xi|\le b$ and any declared fixed small-angle range $(a+b)/z\le\eta_0<1$, where $0<\eta_0<1$, the Fresnel approximation replaces $R=|x-y|$ by $z+|\xi-y_t|^2/(2z)$ and $1/R$ by $1/z$ in the model integral with phase error $O(k(a+b)^4/z^3)$, relative amplitude error $O((a+b)^2/z^2)$ and absolute field error $O(\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}z^{-1}[(a+b)^2/z^2+k(a+b)^4/z^3])$. (c) [Intensity and error transfer] at every $x$ with $x_3>0$ the model period average satisfies $\frac1T\int_0^TU(x,s)^2\,ds=I(x)$ ([[lem-em-period-average]]). If $u_{\rm approx}$ is any approximation of $u$ with $|u_{\rm approx}(x)-u(x)|\le\delta(x)$, then $|\frac12|u_{\rm approx}(x)|^2-I(x)|\le\frac12\delta(x)(|u(x)|+|u_{\rm approx}(x)|)$; if moreover $u(x)\ne0$ and $|u_{\rm approx}(x)-u(x)|\le\epsilon(x)|u(x)|$, the relative intensity error is at most $2\epsilon(x)+\epsilon(x)^2$. In particular the Fraunhofer and Fresnel field errors of (a) and (b) bound the corresponding intensity errors; no new approximation is introduced by passing to $I$. (d) [Trace and scope] the aperture distribution $\alpha$ is an adopted model datum and is not identified with the exact Maxwell boundary data on the screen; assigning both $u$ and $\partial_nu$ on the aperture independently does not produce a well-posed exact boundary problem ([[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]]). The construction ignores polarization and aperture back-reaction, makes no claim that $u$ or $U$ satisfies the Maxwell equations exactly, and makes no measured-intensity, apparatus, sampling or empirical claim; only comparisons of $I$ between observation points are read as model predictions.

[F1] Model interface: the aperture distribution is a finite complex measure with total variation $\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}$ supported in the compact $S$, read in volts; for every $x$ with $x_3>0$ the pairing $\int G_k(x-y)\,d\alpha(y)$ is defined by [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]] and equals the model field $u(x)$; the same formula defines $u$ at every $x\notin S$, and $U$, $I$ are as in the Statement ([[post-em-scalar-aperture-model]], [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]]).

[F6] Elementary toolbox: $|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ for real $\theta$, with $\sin'=\cos$, $\cos'=-\sin$, $|\cos\theta|\le1$ and $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]); the Taylor remainder bound $|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le Ms^{n+1}/(n+1)!$ when $|f^{(n+1)}|\le M$ on the interval, with $R_{n,a}f=f-T_{n,a}f$ ([[cor-taylor-remainder-bound]], [[def-taylor-polynomial-and-remainder]]); the real-power derivatives $(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}$ on $(0,\infty)$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]); the chain and algebra of derivatives ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); the Euclidean norm and inner product with $\sqrt{\ }$ the nonnegative square root ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[thm-of-square-roots]], [[def-complex-exponential]]).

1.1 [Off-support regularity and the Helmholtz equation] Since $S$ is compact and contained in the closed ball of radius $a$, choose the open ball $B_A(0)$ with $A:=a+1$, so that $S\subset B_A(0)$ and $\alpha$ is a finite complex measure supported in that open ball. By [F2] the field $G_k*\alpha$ is $C^\infty$ outside the support of $\alpha$ and solves $(\Delta+k^2)w=0$ there; since the support of $\alpha$ is contained in $S$, the field $u$ of [F1] is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus S$ and satisfies $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ there; the half-space $\{x_3>0\}$ is disjoint from the plane containing $S$, hence is contained in $\mathbb R^3\setminus S$, so $u$ is $C^\infty$ there as well. [given, F1, F2]

1.2 [Elementary bounds: phase, radial expansion, kernel residual] First, for every real $\theta$ one has $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$: by [F6], $2(1-\cos\theta)=|e^{i\theta}-1|^2$ and $|\cos\theta|\le1$, and the Taylor bound for $\cos$ at $0$ with $n=1$ gives $|\cos\theta-1|\le\theta^2/2$, because $|\cos''|\le1$; hence $|e^{i\theta}-1|^2=2(1-\cos\theta)\le\theta^2$. Second, fix $y\in S$, $r\ge2a$, $n\in S^2$, and put $R:=|rn-y|$ and $h(s):=|rn-sy|$ for $s\in[0,1]$; then $h$ is $C^2$ on $[0,1]$ with $h(0)=r$, $h(1)=R$, $h'(0)=-n\cdot y$, $h'(s)=-(rn-sy)\cdot y/h(s)$, $h''(s)=|y|^2/h(s)-((rn-sy)\cdot y)^2/h(s)^3$, so $|h''|\le2|y|^2/h(s)\le2a^2/(r-a)\le4a^2/r$ by $h(s)\ge r-a\ge r/2$; the Taylor bound at $0$ with $n=1$ gives $|R-r+n\cdot y|\le2a^2/r$, and then $|r/R-1|=|r-R|/R\le(a+2a^2/r)/(r/2)=2a/r+4a^2/r^2\le4a/r$ since $|r-R|\le|n\cdot y|+2a^2/r\le a+a=2a$, $R\ge r/2$, and $r\ge2a$ gives $4a^2/r^2\le2a/r$. [step 1.2, F1, F2, F3, F6, algebra]

regularity_scope_evidence: Let $c>0$, let $k\ge2$ be an integer, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open set that is star-shaped with respect to a point $a\in\Omega$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]). Joint regularity on $\Omega\times I$ is read in the restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]]: a map on $\Omega\times I$ is **jointly $C^m$** when it is the restriction of a $C^m$ map on some open neighbourhood of $\Omega\times I$ in $\mathbb R^4$. For open $I$ this is the ordinary open-domain class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] and agrees with the field class of [[def-em-fields]]; for non-open $I$ it is the convention that makes the statements below meaningful, and no time jet is asserted beyond the restricted values.
Let $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ and satisfy the two source-free Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] pointwise on $\Omega\times I$:

with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative $\partial_t$ at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] (at included endpoints of a non-open $I$, as relative derivatives in the restriction convention). Then there are a scalar potential $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ that is jointly $C^{k-1}$ and a vector potential $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is jointly $C^k$, both in the restriction convention, with

so that $(\varphi,A)$ is a potential pair whose field pair is $(E,B)$, in the vocabulary of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]. If $E$ and $B$ are jointly $C^\infty$, then $\varphi$ and $A$ may be chosen jointly $C^\infty$. Conversely, if $\varphi$ and $A$ are jointly $C^\infty$ on $\Omega\times I$ in the restriction convention and $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ are their field pair, then $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ on $\Omega\times I$.

**Given:** A constant $c>0$, an integer $k\ge2$, an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ star-shaped with respect to $a\in\Omega$, an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ with at least two elements, and fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are jointly $C^k$ in the restriction convention and satisfy the two source-free equations of the Statement pointwise.

[F1] Joint regularity and radial witnesses: for an open star-shaped $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with centre $a$ and a jointly $C^m$ field $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, $m\ge1$, with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t\in I$, the radial integral $A(x,t)=\int_0^1s\,B(a+s(x-a),t)\times(x-a)\,ds$ is jointly $C^m$ with $\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$; for a jointly $C^m$ field $C$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$ the negative radial scalar witness $\phi(x,t)=-\int_0^1\langle C(a+s(x-a),t),x-a\rangle\,ds$ is jointly $C^m$ with $\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$; jointly $C^\infty$ data give jointly $C^\infty$ witnesses; and the restriction convention carries the same conclusions at included endpoints of a non-open interval ([[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]]).

[F2] The smooth branch of the adopted vacuum Maxwell equations holds pointwise for jointly $C^1$ fields and contains, among its four equations, $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$; the postulate contains no magnetic charge ([[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]).

[F3] Potential-pair vocabulary: for a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^m$, $m\ge1$, on an open set the electric and magnetic fields are $E(\varphi,A)=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{curl}A$, and both are of class $C^{m-1}$; the definition asserts no existence of potentials for a given field pair ([[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]).

[F4] Euclidean calculus: a map is of class $C^m$ when each component is, the class is closed under sums and compositions of class, and sums, scalar multiples and products of differentiable real functions obey the usual derivative rules ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

[F5] Linearity: for $C^1$ fields $F,G$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and reals $\alpha,\beta$, $\operatorname{curl}(\alpha F+\beta G)=\alpha\operatorname{curl}F+\beta\operatorname{curl}G$, and the divergence is likewise linear ([[lem-divergence-and-curl-are-linear-and-obey-the-scalar-product-rules]]).

[F6] Clairaut--Schwarz: for a $C^2$ function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$ mixed coordinate partial derivatives commute, so for a jointly $C^2$ field the time derivative of each spatial first partial derivative equals the spatial first partial derivative of the time derivative ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]).
[F7] For a $C^2$ field on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ the divergence of its curl vanishes pointwise ([[thm-the-divergence-of-a-curl-vanishes]]).
[F8] For a $C^2$ scalar function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ the curl of its gradient vanishes pointwise ([[thm-the-curl-of-a-gradient-vanishes]]).

[F9] The divergence of a $C^1$ field is $\operatorname{div}F=\sum_i\partial_iF_i$, the curl is $\operatorname{curl}F=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, the gradient is the tuple of first coordinate partial derivatives, and partial derivatives are one-variable derivatives along coordinate lines ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

regularity_scope_evidence: Assume the constant isotropic inertial-rest material branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$, $\sigma\ge0$, $D=\varepsilon E$, $H=B/\mu$, $J_{\rm ext}=0$. The exact broadband physical reading additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$ as in that closure; otherwise the positive coefficients define its finite-band effective phase model without a universal front-speed claim. Put $v^2=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}$ and $\gamma=\sigma/\varepsilon$. The smooth equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with initially zero volume charge give $E_t=v^2\operatorname{curl}B-\gamma E$, $B_t=-\operatorname{curl}E$ and zero divergences; in the finite-energy classes below these first-order equations with the declared PEC weak/variational boundary realization are adopted explicitly, rather than deduced from a smooth-only postulate. The quadratic stored energy is $\mathcal U(t)=\tfrac12(\varepsilon\|E(t)\|_2^2+\mu^{-1}\|B(t)\|_2^2)$, consistent with [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]].

(a) [Rectangular cavity] In the exact zero-normal-$B$ reflection-parity and divergence class of [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] and [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]](c), every initial pair has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ distributional solution of this damped system in the same class. Finite Fourier mode sums converge in energy norm uniformly on compact time intervals and are dense at every time. The Fourier coefficient equations at $k_j=\pi n_j/L_j$ are $\widehat E_t=iv^2 k\times\widehat B-\gamma\widehat E$, $\widehat B_t=-ik\times\widehat E$, with both transverse constraints and the original parities retained.

(b) [Smooth closed PEC cavity] Assume the full Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the smooth spectral and elliptic suppliers. On a bounded smooth cavity $\Omega$, let $X,V,H$ and its smooth orthonormal eigenfields $u_j$, $\lambda_j\ge0$, be exactly [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]] and [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]]. Define the full weak normal-zero divergence-free magnetic space $$M:=\{B\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\int_\Omega B\cdot\nabla\psi=0\text{ for every smooth scalar }\psi\text{ on }\overline\Omega\}.$$ This is the distributional divergence constraint together with weak zero normal flux; for smooth fields it is $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $n\cdot B=0$. For every positive eigenvalue put $w_j=\operatorname{curl}u_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j}$ and put $K_M=\{B\in M:\operatorname{curl}B=0\text{ distributionally}\}$. Then $$M=\overline{\operatorname{span}\{w_j:\lambda_j>0\}}^{L^2}\mathbin{\oplus}K_M.$$ The declared first-order PEC modal energy class is $H\times M$, with weak modal equations $a_j'=v^2\sqrt{\lambda_j}b_j-\gamma a_j$, $b_j'=-\sqrt{\lambda_j}a_j$ for positive modes, $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$ for electric zero modes, and $(B,K_M)'=0$ for every kernel test. Define $D_M$ as the graph-norm completion of finite $w_j$ sums plus $K_M$, with norm squared $\|w\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}w\|_2^2$. The equivalent weak-in-time variational equations are $\langle E_t,\phi\rangle=v^2\langle B,\operatorname{curl}\phi\rangle-\gamma\langle E,\phi\rangle$ for $\phi\in V$, and $\langle B_t,\psi\rangle=-\langle E,\operatorname{curl}\psi\rangle$ for $\psi\in D_M$. They use the actual electric tangential-zero domain $V$ and magnetic normal-zero space $M$, with no claim of maximal-trace equality. For every initial pair in $H\times M$ there is a unique $C(\mathbb R;H\times M)$ solution of that declared realization, which also satisfies the displayed evolution equations distributionally in the interior. Finite electric and paired-magnetic modal sums, with the exact static magnetic kernel component retained, converge uniformly on compact time intervals in energy norm. No equality with every maximal rough tangential-trace realization is asserted.

(c) [Exact energy balance, decay and zero sectors] In both declared classes, for every $t_0<t_1$, $$\mathcal U(t_1)+\sigma\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\|E(t)\|_2^2\,dt=\mathcal U(t_0),\qquad \mathcal U'(t)=-\sigma\|E(t)\|_2^2\le0.$$ For positive smooth-cavity modes $a_j''+\gamma a_j'+v^2\lambda_ja_j=0$. If $\Delta_j=\gamma^2/4-v^2\lambda_j$ is positive, the two roots are $-\gamma/2\pm\sqrt{\Delta_j}$; if negative they are $-\gamma/2\pm i\sqrt{-\Delta_j}$; at zero include $(A+Bt)e^{-\gamma t/2}$. This finite scalar characteristic classification applies to every parameter $\lambda\ge0$ and uses no choice principle; its general zero-eigenvalue associated-wave solutions and the narrower first-order compatibility are stated separately in (d). The full Choice premise belongs to the smooth-cavity spectral realization, not to these finite root formulas. For $\sigma>0$ every positive mode decays, electric zero modes obey $a_j(t)=a_j(0)e^{-\gamma t}$, and magnetic kernel data stay constant. In the smooth class the solution therefore tends in energy norm as $t\to+\infty$ to $(0,P_{K_M}B(0))$. For $\sigma=0$ energy is constant, electric zero modes are static and the original lossless branch is recovered. The zero sectors are retained, not divided by their eigenvalues; no universal decay to zero in the presence of magnetic kernel data is claimed.

(d) [Associated second-order branch] Independently of first-order compatibility, the same spectral basis gives the damped associated electric wave for every $q_0\in V$, $q_1\in H$, with $q\in C(\mathbb R;V)$, $q'\in C(\mathbb R;H)$ and modal convergence uniformly on compact times. Its coefficients satisfy $a_j''+\gamma a_j'+v^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with arbitrary prescribed initial coefficients. At $\lambda_j=0$ they are $\alpha_j+\beta_j(1-e^{-\gamma t})/\gamma$ when $\gamma>0$, and $\alpha_j+t\beta_j$ when $\gamma=0$. Such arbitrary second-order data need not arise from the first-order Maxwell system: its zero modes additionally satisfy $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$. This broader wave is retained alongside the physical first-order branch. All square roots and real derivatives use [[thm-of-square-roots]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] and the real-component exponential formula [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]].

(e) [Scope] The conductor occupies the declared cavity interior while its stationary walls obey the independent ideal PEC boundary model. No arbitrary loss tensor, memory law, changing interface, open-end, rough-wall or empirical conclusion is made. Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) suffices for the rectangular/Fourier branch; the smooth branch retains its actual full Choice premise. Weak energy balance is proved by modal limits and does not assert an unprovided nonlinear weak local Poynting theorem.

**Given:** The constant isotropic inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] with constants $\varepsilon,\mu>0$, $\sigma\ge0$, relations $D=\varepsilon E$, $H=B/\mu$, $J_{\rm ext}=0$ (the isotropic broadband condition $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$ is additional and is not used); the smooth equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with initially zero volume charge; the PEC guide/cavity geometry and weak reflection class of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]]; $v^2:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}$ and $\gamma:=\sigma/\varepsilon$.

1.1 [Rectangular damped modal system] Assume Countable Choice. Fix the box $Q$ and the reflection class of [F2], and let $(E,B)$ be a $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ distributional solution of the damped first-order system of [F1] in that class. The finite separated Fourier modes are dense in the class by [F2], and for a wavevector $k\in(\pi/L_1)\mathbb Z\times(\pi/L_2)\mathbb Z\times(\pi/L_3)\mathbb Z$ the coefficient system of the damped system reads $\widehat E_t=iv^2\,k\times\widehat B-\gamma\widehat E$, $\widehat B_t=-ik\times\widehat E$: this is [F2]'s recorded coefficient system with the additional scalar term $-\gamma\widehat E$ of [F1], and the algebraic constraint $k\cdot(k\times w)=0$ preserves $k\cdot\widehat E=k\cdot\widehat B=0$, while the finite Fourier modes carry the parities of the class because the reflection rules are diagonal in the separated basis. [F1, F2]

2.1 [Rectangular class: global solutions, energy and convergence] For every initial pair in the rectangular class of [F2] the damped system of [F1] has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ distributional solution in the class, finite Fourier mode sums converge in energy norm uniformly on compact time intervals and are dense at every time, and the coefficient equations of step 1.1 hold for every wavevector. Indeed, for each $k$ the right-hand side of the finite-dimensional system of step 1.1 is globally state-Lipschitz (it is affine), so [F7] gives a unique global solution through the initial coefficients; differentiating the per-mode energy $\varepsilon|\widehat E|^2+\mu^{-1}|\widehat B|^2$ and using $\operatorname{Re}(\overline{\widehat E}\cdot(k\times\widehat B))+$ its conjugate $=0$ (the scalar triple-product identity of [F8] with complex conjugation, [F9]) gives $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\varepsilon|\widehat E|^2+\mu^{-1}|\widehat B|^2\bigr)=-2\sigma|\widehat E|^2\le0$, so each modal energy is nonincreasing forward and bounded by $e^{2\gamma T}$ times its initial value on $[-T,T]$ (multiply by $e^{2\gamma t}$ and differentiate); Parseval for the complete class [F2] therefore controls the energy-norm of every omitted tail uniformly on compact times. Finite solutions converge in $C_tL^2$ to a limit in the class, and the linear distributional equations pass to the limit against compactly supported smooth periodic tests by Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] on a compact time support, exactly as in the lossless argument of [F2]; the constraints $k\cdot\widehat E=k\cdot\widehat B=0$ and the parities are preserved by step 1.1, so the limit lies in the same class. Uniqueness: a $C_tL^2$ weak solution has continuous coefficients whose distributional derivatives equal the displayed continuous right-hand sides; for each coefficient equation, subtract the oriented primitive of the continuous right-hand side, which is $C^1$ with that derivative by [F6], use the $C^1$ regular-distribution compatibility of [F6] to identify its distributional derivative, conclude that the difference has zero distributional derivative, hence is constant by [F6], and match the initial value; global uniqueness of the finite system identifies the coefficients, and completeness of the Fourier class identifies the fields. [step 1.1, F2, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9]

3.1 [Smooth PEC cavity: modal system, variational equations and uniqueness] Assume the full Axiom of Choice as in [F3]. Let $H\times M$ be the energy class of steps 1.2, with $M=\overline{\operatorname{span}\{w_j\}}\oplus K_M$. For coefficients $a_j=(\cdot,u_j)$, $b_j=(\cdot,w_j)$ declare the first-order modal system $a_j'=v^2\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,b_j-\gamma a_j$, $b_j'=-\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,a_j$ for $\lambda_j>0$, and $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$ for the electric zero modes, and declare the magnetic kernel data constant, $(B,K_M)'=0$ for every kernel test. Endow the paired-magnetic space with the completion $D_M$ of finite $w_j$-sums plus $K_M$ for the norm $\|w\|_{D_M}^2:=\|w\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}w\|_2^2$, and consider the weak variational equations $\langle E_t,\phi\rangle=v^2\langle B,\operatorname{curl}\phi\rangle-\gamma\langle E,\phi\rangle$ for $\phi\in V$ and $\langle B_t,\psi\rangle=-\langle E,\operatorname{curl}\psi\rangle$ for $\psi\in D_M$. Then every initial pair in $H\times M$ has a unique $C(\mathbb R;H\times M)$ solution of this declared realization, it satisfies the modal equations distributionally, and finite electric and paired-magnetic modal sums together with the static kernel component converge uniformly on compact time intervals in energy norm. Existence and uniqueness are finite-dimensional: each paired system is a globally Lipschitz constant-coefficient system solved by [F7], and the kernel data are constant, so a candidate solution is the norm-limit of its finite modal sums; the sums converge because the energy $\sum_j(\varepsilon|a_j|^2+\mu^{-1}|b_j|^2)$ is controlled as in step 2.1 and the kernel component is retained exactly. For the variational equations, the finite sums satisfy them against finite spectral tests by the full-$X$ identity of [F3], and the density of the finite spectral tests in $V$ and in $D_M$ passes the identities to the limit by Cauchy–Schwarz [F5], since uniform energy convergence on compact times controls both pairings. Conversely, testing the variational equations against $u_j$ (for $\phi$) and $w_j$ or kernel vectors (for $\psi$) recovers the modal equations, so the weak realization and the modal system are equivalent in the stated class; uniqueness follows from the scalar ODE uniqueness and the complete decomposition of step 1.2. For strong first-order solutions with $E\in C^1_tH\cap C_tV$ and $B\in C^1_tL^2\cap C_tH(\operatorname{curl})$, the same pairing gives $a_j'=v^2(B,\operatorname{curl}u_j)-\gamma a_j$ and, differentiating with $B'=-\operatorname{curl}E$ and the full-$X$ identity, $a_j''+\gamma a_j'+v^2\lambda_j a_j=0$ with $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$ at $\lambda_j=0$. No maximal rough tangential-trace realisation is claimed. [step 1.2, F3, F5, F7]

4.1 [Exact energy balance] In both declared classes, for every $t_0<t_1$, $\mathcal U(t_1)+\sigma\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\|E(t)\|_2^2dt=\mathcal U(t_0)$ and $\mathcal U'(t)=-\sigma\|E(t)\|_2^2\le0$. In the rectangular class, sum the finite per-mode identities of step 2.1 over the wavevectors of a finite modal projection, integrate over $[t_0,t_1]$ with [F6], and pass to the limit using the uniform energy-norm convergence of step 2.1 to pass both the energy and the continuous $\|E(t)\|_2^2$-integral terms; in the smooth class, do the same with the paired modal energies of step 3.1 and the retained kernel component, whose curl vanishes. The derivative form then follows from the integral form by [F6]; the boundary term of a smooth local Poynting identity is not used, so no unprovided nonlinear weak local identity is asserted. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F6]

4.2 [Associated second-order branch] Independently of first-order compatibility, the same spectral basis gives the damped associated electric wave for every $q_0\in V$, $q_1\in H$, with $q\in C(\mathbb R;V)$, $q'\in C(\mathbb R;H)$ and modal convergence uniform on compact times: its coefficients satisfy $a_j''+\gamma a_j'+v^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with prescribed initial coefficients $a_j(0)=(q_0,u_j)$, $a_j'(0)=(q_1,u_j)$, and at $\lambda_j=0$ they are $\alpha_j+\beta_j(1-e^{-\gamma t})/\gamma$ for $\gamma>0$ and $\alpha_j+t\beta_j$ for $\gamma=0$. Indeed, for $\lambda_j>0$ the function $Q_j=|a_j'|^2+v^2\lambda_j|a_j|^2$ satisfies $Q_j'=-2\gamma|a_j'|^2\le0$ by [F7], and the positive eigenvalues, being finite in multiplicity and tending to infinity, have a positive lower bound, so compact-time exponential bounds on $Q_j$ control the $V$ displacement and $H$ velocity tails by the weighted $V$-norm identity of [F3]; the finitely many zero modes have the displayed solutions by step 1.3, and the finite-sum FTC estimate of [F6] passes the $H$ derivative to the limit and identifies the variational second-order equation against compact-time tests. Such arbitrary second-order data need not arise from the first-order Maxwell system: its zero modes additionally satisfy $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$, and the broader wave is retained alongside the physical first-order branch. about a fixed position $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$. The family time interval $I$ is not required to contain a full period, and no solution $r_\eta$ outside $I$ is assumed. For the periodic-response conclusions (b), (c), impose the following explicit preparation (P): the unique global harmonic-ODE extension of $r_1$ supplied after (a) by [[lem-em-harmonic-forcing-periodic-response]](d), with its actual value and derivative at $0$, is $T$-periodic, $T=2\pi/\omega$.
